recipes.title: Crushed tomatoes, water-bath canned
recipes.tagline: The plainest, most useful jar in the pantry: tomatoes and nothing else, ready for any sauce in February.
recipes.makes: About 7 × 1 L (quart) jars from 10 kg (22 lb) of tomatoes; 6.4 kg (14 lb) fills 9 × 500 ml (pint) jars
safety: The lemon juice is not optional: tomatoes sit near pH 4.6 and the added acid is what makes a boiling-water bath safe. Use bottled juice, not fresh — the acidity of fresh lemons varies.
Do not add onions, peppers, celery, garlic or oil — that is a different, low-acid recipe and needs a tested salsa or pressure-canning recipe.
A little sugar may be added to soften the acid taste, but never leave the acid out.
Use only jars made for canning with new two-piece lids; a sealed lid is concave and does not flex.
Skip tomatoes from frost-killed or dead vines and anything soft or mouldy — they can be less acidic and spoil the batch.

source.label: NCHFP: Crushed Tomatoes (with no added liquid)

ingredients: 10 kg (22 lb) ripe paste or slicing tomatoes — reckon about 1.25 kg (2¾ lb) per litre jar
Bottled lemon juice: 2 tablespoons (30 ml) per 1 L jar, 1 tablespoon (15 ml) per 500 ml jar — or citric acid, ½ teaspoon per 1 L jar, ¼ teaspoon per 500 ml jar
Salt, optional: 1 teaspoon (5 ml) per 1 L jar, for flavour only

process.altitude: 500 ml jars: 35 min. For both sizes add 5 min at 300–900 m (1,001–3,000 ft), 10 min at 900–1,800 m (3,001–6,000 ft), 15 min above 1,800 m (6,000 ft).

steps: Wash the jars and keep them hot in the canner while the water heats; wash the lids in hot soapy water and set them aside. A child can wash and sort the tomatoes while you set up.
Dip the tomatoes in boiling water 30–60 seconds until the skins split, then into cold water. Slip the skins, cut out the cores and trim any bruises or black spots. Quarter them.

Put about a sixth of the quarters in a large pot and crush them with a masher while heating hard and stirring, so they give up their juice and come to the boil. Add the rest a few handfuls at a time, stirring constantly — these don’t need crushing, they soften in the hot juice. Once everything is in, boil gently 5 minutes.
Put the lemon juice (or citric acid) into each hot jar first — 2 tablespoons per litre, 1 per 500 ml — and the salt if you are using it.

Fill the jars with hot tomatoes, leaving 1.25 cm (½ inch) headspace. Run a chopstick down the inside to free bubbles, top up if needed, wipe the rims, centre the lids and screw the bands on fingertip-tight.

Lower the jars into the canner so the water covers them by at least 5 cm (2 inches). Bring to a full rolling boil, then start the clock: 1 L jars 45 minutes, 500 ml jars 35 minutes at 0–300 m. Keep it boiling the whole time; if it stops, bring it back and start the clock again.

Turn off the heat, take off the lid and wait 5 minutes. Lift the jars straight up onto a towel and leave them 12–24 hours untouched. Press each lid: a sealed one is concave and does not spring back. Refrigerate any that did not seal and use within a week.
recipes.keeps: 12–18 months in a cool dark cupboard, best within a year. Refrigerate after opening and use within a week.
recipes.variations: Paste tomatoes (Roma, San Marzano, Amish Paste) give a thicker jar; slicers give more juice. For a smooth purée, pass the hot tomatoes through a food mill and can them as tomato juice instead (its own times, below).

recipes.title: Whole or halved tomatoes in juice, water-bath canned
recipes.tagline: Whole peeled tomatoes under their own juice — the jar you open for a winter stew when you want pieces, not purée.
recipes.makes: 7 × 1 L (quart) jars from 9.5 kg (21 lb) of tomatoes, plus extra tomatoes for the juice; 5.9 kg (13 lb) fills 9 × 500 ml (pint) jars
safety: Acid goes in every jar before the tomatoes — the 85 minutes is about how slowly heat reaches the centre of a tight-packed jar, and it assumes the lemon juice or citric acid is there.
The 85 minutes is for tomatoes covered in tomato juice. Tomatoes packed in water or with no added liquid are different recipes with different times; do not mix them up.
Keep the jars under at least 5 cm of boiling water for the whole 85 minutes and restart the clock if the boil stops.
No onions, peppers, celery or herbs in the jar; season when you cook with them in winter.

source.label: NCHFP: Whole or Halved Tomatoes (packed in tomato juice)

ingredients: 9.5 kg (21 lb) firm ripe tomatoes, small to medium so they fit through the jar mouth
Tomato juice to cover — about 2–3 L, pressed from an extra 3–4 kg (7–9 lb) of soft tomatoes by the tomato-juice method (heat, crush, press through a food mill)
Bottled lemon juice: 2 tablespoons (30 ml) per 1 L jar, 1 tablespoon (15 ml) per 500 ml jar — or citric acid, ½ teaspoon per 1 L jar, ¼ teaspoon per 500 ml jar
Salt, optional: 1 teaspoon (5 ml) per 1 L jar
steps: Make the juice first from your softest tomatoes: quarter, heat and crush them in a pot, simmer 5 minutes, press through a food mill and keep hot. Set the washed jars in the canner to heat; wash the lids and set aside.

Wash the tomatoes for the jars — a child’s job — then dip them in boiling water 30–60 seconds until the skins split and drop them into cold water. Slip the skins and cut out the cores. Leave whole, or halve the big ones.
Put the lemon juice (or citric acid) into each hot jar, with salt if you like.
Hot pack: put the peeled tomatoes in a large pot, pour in enough hot juice to cover them completely and boil gently 5 minutes.

Fill the jars with the hot tomatoes to 1.25 cm (½ inch) from the rim, then ladle in hot juice to cover them, keeping that 1.25 cm headspace. Slide a chopstick around the inside to free bubbles, wipe the rims, centre the lids and screw the bands on fingertip-tight.

Lower the jars into the canner with water at least 5 cm (2 inches) over the lids — this is a long process and the level drops. Bring to a full rolling boil, then time it: 85 minutes for both 1 L and 500 ml jars at 0–300 m. Add boiling water around (not onto) the jars if the level falls.
Turn off the heat, uncover, wait 5 minutes, then lift the jars onto a towel. Leave 12–24 hours; check that every lid is concave and firm. Refrigerate any that did not seal and use within a week.
recipes.keeps: 12–18 months in a cool dark cupboard. Refrigerate after opening and use within a week.
recipes.variations: The same page gives a raw pack — raw peeled tomatoes in the jar with hot juice poured over, same headspace and the same 85 minutes — which is quicker on the stove but floats more and loses more liquid.

recipes.title: Plain tomato sauce, water-bath canned
recipes.tagline: Unseasoned tomato sauce boiled down from juice — thin for soups, thick for pasta — with every flavour decision left for the day you open it.
recipes.makes: About 7 × 1 L (quart) jars of thin sauce from 16 kg (35 lb) of tomatoes, or of thick sauce from 21 kg (46 lb); for 9 × 500 ml (pint) jars use 9.5 kg (21 lb) thin or 12.7 kg (28 lb) thick
safety: Acid in every jar, measured, before the sauce goes in. Boiling the sauce down concentrates the tomato but does not make it acidic enough on its own.
This is plain sauce: no onion, garlic, peppers, herbs, oil or thickeners. Seasoned ‘spaghetti sauce’ is a low-acid mixture with its own tested pressure-canning recipe.
Headspace is a tight 6 mm (¼ inch) for sauce, less than for crushed tomatoes — measure it.
Keep the sauce at a boil when you fill the jars; a cooled, thick sauce heats slowly in the canner.
ingredients: 16 kg (35 lb) ripe tomatoes for thin sauce, or 21 kg (46 lb) for thick sauce — paste tomatoes cook down fastest
Bottled lemon juice: 2 tablespoons (30 ml) per 1 L jar, 1 tablespoon (15 ml) per 500 ml jar — or citric acid, ½ teaspoon per 1 L jar, ¼ teaspoon per 500 ml jar
Salt, optional: 1 teaspoon (5 ml) per 1 L jar

process.altitude: 1 L jars: 40 min. For both sizes add 5 min at 300–900 m (1,001–3,000 ft), 10 min at 900–1,800 m (3,001–6,000 ft), 15 min above 1,800 m (6,000 ft).

steps: Wash the tomatoes (a child can do this), cut out stems and any bruised or dark patches. Quarter about 500 g into a large pot and heat hard while crushing them; as it boils, keep adding and crushing quarters so the pot never stops boiling. Simmer 5 minutes once everything is in.
Press the hot pulp through a food mill or sieve to take out skins and seeds. Pour the juice into the widest pot you own — a wide pot evaporates faster.

Simmer, stirring now and then so it does not catch, until the volume has dropped by a third for thin sauce or by half for thick sauce. Mark the starting level on a wooden spoon handle so you can tell. This takes an hour or more.
Set the washed jars to heat in the canner and wash the lids. Put the lemon juice (or citric acid) into each hot jar, plus salt if you like.
Fill the jars with boiling-hot sauce, leaving only 6 mm (¼ inch) headspace. Free any bubbles with a chopstick, wipe the rims, centre the lids and screw the bands on fingertip-tight.
Lower into the canner with at least 5 cm (2 inches) of water over the lids, bring to a full rolling boil and time it: 500 ml jars 35 minutes, 1 L jars 40 minutes at 0–300 m.
Turn off the heat, uncover, wait 5 minutes, lift the jars onto a towel and leave 12–24 hours. Check the seals; refrigerate any that failed and use within a week.
recipes.keeps: 12–18 months in a cool dark cupboard. Refrigerate after opening and use within 5–7 days.
recipes.variations: Thin sauce (reduced by a third) is the better all-rounder — thicken it in the pan in winter. If a smooth texture matters less, make the crushed-tomatoes recipe instead and use its headspace and times (1.25 cm; 500 ml 35 min, 1 L 45 min).

recipes.title: Choice salsa, water-bath canned
recipes.tagline: The tested salsa that lets you choose the peppers and onions — mild or fierce — as long as the measured cups and the lemon juice stay exactly as written.
recipes.makes: About 6 × 500 ml (pint) jars
safety: Measure everything in metric or everything in US cups — never mix the two, or the acid ratio shifts.

What may not change: 6 cups tomatoes, 9 cups onions and/or peppers, 1½ cups bottled lemon or lime juice. These proportions were tested with many kinds of tomato, pepper and onion; shift them and the salsa may not be acidic enough for a boiling-water bath.
What may change: which peppers (bell, jalapeño, habanero, any colour) and the onion-to-pepper split, as long as the total stays at 9 cups.
Do not substitute vinegar for the lemon or lime juice, and do not use bottled key lime juice. Fresh citrus varies in acidity; the bottled juice standardizes it.
No other vegetables (corn, beans, carrots, garlic) and no thickeners, flour or cornstarch — they were not tested. Season at the table with cilantro, cumin or garlic rather than in the jar.
Wear gloves for hot peppers and keep hands away from eyes — and keep small helpers on tomato and onion duty.
ingredients: 1.5 L (6 cups) peeled, cored, seeded and chopped ripe tomatoes — about 2 kg (4½ lb) whole, measured level in dry measuring cups
2.25 L (9 cups) diced onions and/or peppers, any mix: sweet bell peppers of any colour, hot peppers, or both — measured level in dry measuring cups
375 ml (1½ cups) commercially bottled lemon or lime juice, measured in a liquid measuring cup
15 ml (3 teaspoons) canning or pickling salt

process.altitude: Both sizes: 20 min at 300–1,800 m (1,001–6,000 ft), 25 min above 1,800 m (6,000 ft).

steps: Set 6 washed 500 ml jars (or 12 × 250 ml) to heat in the canner and wash the lids. Peel and dice the onions into 6 mm (¼ inch) pieces. Wash and core the bell peppers, strip out seeds and membranes, and dice the same size.
Wear gloves for the hot peppers. Stem them, keep or discard as many seeds and membranes as the heat you want, and dice 6 mm. Measure the onions and peppers together: 9 level cups, no more, no less.

Dip the tomatoes in boiling water 30–60 seconds until the skins split, then into cold water. Peel, core, squeeze or scoop out the seeds and chop into 6 mm–1.25 cm pieces. Measure 6 level cups. A child can measure and level the cups.
Combine the vegetables in a large pot with the lemon juice and salt. Bring to a boil over medium heat, stirring, then lower the heat and simmer 3 minutes, stirring so it does not scorch.

Ladle the hot salsa into the hot jars, leaving 1.25 cm (½ inch) headspace. Free bubbles with a chopstick and top up to the same headspace, wipe the rims with a damp paper towel, centre the lids and screw the bands on fingertip-tight.
Lower the jars into the canner with at least 5 cm (2 inches) of water over the lids, bring to a full rolling boil and process 15 minutes for 500 ml or 250 ml jars at 0–300 m.

Turn off the heat, uncover, wait 5 minutes and lift the jars onto a towel. Leave 12–24 hours, check the seals, and refrigerate any that did not seal — plus whatever did not fit in a jar — to eat fresh.
recipes.keeps: 12–18 months in a cool dark cupboard. Refrigerate once opened and use within a week.
recipes.variations: Paste tomatoes give a thicker salsa than slicers. Go all sweet peppers for a salsa children will eat, or make the 9 cups mostly jalapeño for a hot one — the process time is the same.

recipes.title: Tomato juice, water-bath canned
recipes.tagline: A clear use for a glut of soft, juicy slicers: hot-pressed juice that will not separate in the jar.
recipes.makes: About 7 × 1 L (quart) jars from 10.4 kg (23 lb) of tomatoes; 6.4 kg (14 lb) fills 9 × 500 ml (pint) jars
safety: Acid in every jar, measured, before the juice — tomato juice is canned in boiling water only because the lemon juice or citric acid is added.
Plain tomato only. Adding celery, onion, peppers or carrot makes a vegetable-juice blend, which has its own tested recipe and limits.
Fresh, firm, ripe tomatoes; none from frost-killed vines and nothing going soft.
A little sugar can balance the acid taste if you like, but the acid itself never comes out.
ingredients: 10.4 kg (23 lb) ripe juicy tomatoes — about 1.5 kg (3¼ lb) per litre jar
Bottled lemon juice: 2 tablespoons (30 ml) per 1 L jar, 1 tablespoon (15 ml) per 500 ml jar — or citric acid, ½ teaspoon per 1 L jar, ¼ teaspoon per 500 ml jar
Salt, optional: 1 teaspoon (5 ml) per 1 L jar

process.altitude: 1 L jars: 40 min. For both sizes add 5 min at 300–900 m (1,001–3,000 ft), 10 min at 900–1,800 m (3,001–6,000 ft), 15 min above 1,800 m (6,000 ft).

steps: Set the washed jars to heat in the canner and wash the lids. Wash the tomatoes — a good job for a child at the sink — pull the stems and trim away any bruised or dark spots.

To keep the juice from separating, work fast and hot: quarter about 500 g (1 lb) straight into a large pot and bring to a boil while crushing with a masher. Keep cutting quarters and adding them to the boiling pot, crushing as you go, so it never drops below a hard boil. Once all the tomatoes are in, simmer 5 minutes.
Press the hot pulp through a food mill or sieve to remove skins and seeds. Return the juice to the pot and bring it back to a boil.
Put the lemon juice (or citric acid) into each hot jar, plus salt if you like.
Fill the jars with boiling juice, leaving 1.25 cm (½ inch) headspace. Wipe the rims, centre the lids and screw the bands on fingertip-tight.
Lower into the canner with at least 5 cm (2 inches) of water over the lids, bring to a full rolling boil and time it: 500 ml jars 35 minutes, 1 L jars 40 minutes at 0–300 m.
Turn off the heat, uncover, wait 5 minutes, lift the jars onto a towel and leave them 12–24 hours. Check the seals; refrigerate any that did not seal and drink within a few days.
recipes.keeps: 12–18 months in a cool dark cupboard. Refrigerate after opening and use within 5–7 days.
recipes.variations: If you do not mind the juice separating into a clear layer and pulp, simply quarter all the tomatoes into the pot, crush, heat and simmer 5 minutes before pressing — the same times apply. Shake the jar before pouring.

recipes.title: Quick fresh-pack dill pickles
recipes.tagline: Kosher-style dills without the weeks of fermenting: an overnight salt soak, a hot spiced brine, and a short bath.
recipes.makes: 7–9 × 500 ml (pint) jars
recipes.total: 12-hour soak plus 1½ hours, then 12–24 hours cooling
safety: Vinegar must be 5% acidity and the vinegar-to-water ratio of the brine stays as written; do not dilute it to soften the sourness.
Use canning or pickling salt — table salt clouds the brine. If you want less salt, follow one of the NCHFP’s tested reduced-sodium pickle recipes rather than trimming this one.
Trim the blossom end; it carries enzymes that turn pickles soft.
Garlic, hot pepper and extra spice are not in this tested recipe. If you want garlic dills, use a tested recipe that includes garlic rather than adding cloves to this one.
Every cucumber stays below the brine; a jar with a cucumber poking out of the liquid is a jar to refrigerate and eat first.
ingredients: 3.6 kg (8 lb) pickling cucumbers, 7.5–12.5 cm (3–5 inches) long
For the overnight soak: 7.5 L (2 US gallons) water and 175 ml (¾ cup) canning or pickling salt
For the brine: 1.5 L (6 cups) vinegar (5%), 2 L (8 cups) water, 125 ml (½ cup) canning or pickling salt, 60 ml (¼ cup) sugar
30 ml (2 tablespoons) whole mixed pickling spice, tied in a square of clean cloth
Whole mustard seed: 1 teaspoon (5 ml) per jar — about 45 ml (3 tablespoons) in all
Fresh dill: 1½ heads per jar, about 14 heads — or dill seed, 1½ teaspoons (7 ml) per jar
steps: The evening before: wash the cucumbers well (children are good at this) and cut a 2 mm (1/16 inch) slice off each blossom end — it holds an enzyme that softens pickles — leaving 6 mm (¼ inch) of stem. Dissolve 175 ml salt in 7.5 L water, pour it over the cucumbers in a food-grade bucket or crock, and leave 12 hours.
Next day, drain the cucumbers. Wash 9 × 500 ml jars and keep them hot; wash the lids and set aside. Fill the canner and heat the water to about 60 °C (140 °F) for a raw pack.
Make the brine: combine the vinegar, 125 ml salt, sugar and 1.9 L water in a large pot, drop in the bag of pickling spice and bring to a boil.
Pack the cucumbers upright into the hot jars, snug but not crushed — a child can stand them in. Add 1 teaspoon mustard seed and 1½ heads of dill (or 1½ teaspoons dill seed) to each jar.

Pour the boiling brine over the cucumbers, leaving 1.25 cm (½ inch) headspace and making sure every cucumber is under the brine. Free bubbles with a chopstick, wipe the rims, centre the lids and screw the bands on fingertip-tight.
Lower into the canner with at least 5 cm (2 inches) of water over the lids, bring to a full rolling boil and process 500 ml jars 10 minutes (1 L jars 15 minutes) at 0–300 m.
Turn off the heat, uncover, wait 5 minutes and lift the jars onto a towel. Leave 12–24 hours, check the seals, and give them 4–6 weeks in the cupboard to turn into proper dills.
recipes.keeps: 12 months in a cool dark cupboard; crispest in the first six. Refrigerate after opening and eat within a month or two.
recipes.variations: The source also allows a low-temperature pasteurization instead of the boiling bath — holding the jars in 82–85 °C (180–185 °F) water for 30 minutes, checked with a thermometer the whole time — which gives a crisper pickle but is easy to get wrong; stick with the boiling bath for a first batch.

recipes.title: Bread-and-butter pickles
recipes.tagline: Sweet, turmeric-yellow cucumber and onion slices — the pickle most children will actually eat, and the one that uses up the big cucumbers.
recipes.makes: About 8 × 500 ml (pint) jars
recipes.total: 5 hours including the ice soak, plus 12–24 hours cooling
safety: The 1 L of 5% vinegar to 2.7 kg of cucumbers and 2 L of onions is the tested ratio — the sugar can be cut only by following a tested reduced-sugar recipe, and the vinegar is never cut.
Pickling or canning salt for the ice soak; drain well, or the syrup ends up watery.
The jars are hot-packed — bring the slices back to a boil with the syrup before filling, so the 10 minutes in the canner is enough.
Skip the pickling-lime firming option on the source page unless you follow its three rinses exactly; the crushed-ice soak is the simple way to crisp slices.
ingredients: 2.7 kg (6 lb) pickling cucumbers, 10–12.5 cm (4–5 inches) long
2 L (8 cups) thinly sliced onions — about 1.4 kg (3 lb)
125 ml (½ cup) canning or pickling salt
1 L (4 cups) vinegar (5%)
900 g (4½ cups) sugar
30 ml (2 tablespoons) mustard seed
22 ml (1½ tablespoons) celery seed
15 ml (1 tablespoon) ground turmeric
Plenty of crushed or cubed ice

process.altitude: Both sizes: 15 min at 300–1,800 m (1,001–6,000 ft), 20 min above 1,800 m (6,000 ft).

steps: Wash the cucumbers and cut 2 mm (1/16 inch) off each blossom end. Slice them 5 mm (3/16 inch) thick — a mandoline makes this even — and slice the onions thinly.
Toss the cucumbers and onions with the salt in a big bowl, bury them under 5 cm (2 inches) of ice and refrigerate 3–4 hours, adding ice as it melts. Then drain them well.
Set 8 washed 500 ml jars to heat in the canner and wash the lids.
Combine the vinegar, sugar, mustard seed, celery seed and turmeric in a large pot and boil 10 minutes. Add the drained cucumbers and onions and bring slowly back to a boil, stirring gently.

Fill the hot jars with slices and the hot syrup, leaving 1.25 cm (½ inch) headspace. Free bubbles with a chopstick, top up with syrup if needed, wipe the rims, centre the lids and screw the bands on fingertip-tight.
Lower into the canner with at least 5 cm (2 inches) of water over the lids, bring to a full rolling boil and process 10 minutes for 500 ml or 1 L jars at 0–300 m.
Turn off the heat, uncover, wait 5 minutes and lift the jars onto a towel. Leave 12–24 hours and check the seals. Let them sit 4–5 weeks before opening; the flavour needs the time.
recipes.keeps: 12 months in a cool dark cupboard. Refrigerate after opening and eat within a couple of months.
recipes.variations: Squash bread-and-butters: swap slender zucchini or yellow summer squash, 2.5–4 cm (1–1½ inches) across, for the cucumbers — same quantities, same times. The lime variation is not for squash.

recipes.title: Dilly beans (pickled green beans)
recipes.tagline: Whole beans standing to attention in a garlicky dill brine — the first jar most families let the children pack.
recipes.makes: About 8 × 500 ml (pint) jars
safety: Equal parts 5% vinegar and water, with the salt as written, is the tested brine; do not weaken it, and do not add more water to stretch it.
Because the process is only 5 minutes, the jars must be sterilized in boiling water for 10 minutes first — a hot jar from the dishwasher is not enough.
One clove of garlic per jar is the tested amount; garlic is a low-acid vegetable and more of it was not tested.
Pints only. Quarts hold more cold bean in the middle and no time has been established for them.
Beans must be young and tender; tough, stringy late beans stay tough in the jar.
ingredients: 1.8 kg (4 lb) fresh tender green or yellow beans, 12–15 cm (5–6 inches) long
8–16 heads of fresh dill (1–2 per jar)
8 cloves garlic, optional (1 per jar)
125 ml (½ cup) canning or pickling salt
1 L (4 cups) white vinegar (5%)
1 L (4 cups) water
5 ml (1 teaspoon) hot red pepper flakes, optional

process.altitude: 10 min at 300–1,800 m (1,001–6,000 ft), 15 min above 1,800 m (6,000 ft). No tested time for 1 L jars — use pints.

steps: Sterilize the jars, because the process is under 10 minutes: stand 8 × 500 ml jars upright on the rack in the canner, fill the canner and jars with hot water to 2.5 cm (1 inch) above the rims, and boil 10 minutes (one minute more for each 300 m above sea level). Leave them in the hot water until you fill them. Wash the lids and set aside.
Wash the beans and snap or trim the ends — snapping is a job a four-year-old takes seriously. Cut them to 10 cm (4 inch) lengths, so they stand below the jar’s shoulder.
Lift out a jar, drain it, and drop in 1–2 dill heads and a garlic clove if using. Stand the beans upright in the jar, packed close, leaving 1.25 cm (½ inch) headspace. Trim any that stand too tall.
Combine the salt, vinegar, water and pepper flakes in a pot and bring to a boil.

Pour the boiling brine over the beans, leaving 1.25 cm (½ inch) headspace and making sure the beans are covered. Free bubbles with a chopstick, wipe the rims, centre the lids and screw the bands on fingertip-tight.
Lower into the canner with at least 5 cm (2 inches) of water over the lids, bring to a full rolling boil and process 500 ml jars 5 minutes at 0–300 m.
Turn off the heat, uncover, wait 5 minutes and lift the jars onto a towel. Leave 12–24 hours and check the seals. Wait at least two weeks before opening so the brine gets into the beans.
recipes.keeps: 12 months in a cool dark cupboard. Refrigerate after opening and eat within a month.
recipes.variations: Yellow wax beans and green beans can be mixed in one jar for colour. Skip the pepper flakes for a jar the children will eat with their fingers.

recipes.title: Pickled beets
recipes.tagline: Sweet-sour beet slices with cinnamon and clove — the pickle that makes a winter plate look like something.
recipes.makes: About 8 × 500 ml (pint) jars
safety: Beets are a low-acid vegetable; only the 1 L of 5% vinegar to 500 ml of water makes them a boiling-water job. Never add more water or beet cooking liquid to the brine.
Discard the water the beets were cooked in — the recipe is written with fresh water in the pickling liquid.
The 30 minutes is longer than most pickles because beet slices are dense; do not shorten it for small jars.
Onions are the only extra the recipe allows; stick to the amount given or leave them out.
ingredients: 3.2 kg (7 lb) beets, 5–6 cm (2–2½ inches) across
1 L (4 cups) vinegar (5%)
7 ml (1½ teaspoons) canning or pickling salt
400 g (2 cups) sugar
500 ml (2 cups) fresh water
2 cinnamon sticks
12 whole cloves
4–6 small onions, 5–6 cm across, optional
steps: Cut the beet tops off leaving 2.5 cm (1 inch) of stem, and leave the root on, so they do not bleed their colour while cooking. Scrub them well — a child with a vegetable brush is ideal — and sort by size.

Cover beets of a similar size with boiling water and cook until tender, about 25–30 minutes. Drain and throw the cooking water away — it does not go in the jars. Let the beets cool enough to handle, trim roots and stems, slip the skins off with your thumbs and slice 6 mm (¼ inch) thick. Peel and thinly slice the onions.
Set 8 washed 500 ml jars to heat in the canner and wash the lids.

Combine the vinegar, salt, sugar and 500 ml fresh water in a large pot. Tie the cinnamon and cloves in a square of cloth and drop it in. Bring to a boil, add the beets and onions and simmer 5 minutes. Fish out the spice bag.

Fill the hot jars with beets and onions, leaving 1.25 cm (½ inch) headspace, then ladle in the hot liquid to the same headspace. Free bubbles with a chopstick, wipe the rims, centre the lids and screw the bands on fingertip-tight.
Lower into the canner with at least 5 cm (2 inches) of water over the lids, bring to a full rolling boil and process 30 minutes for 500 ml or 1 L jars at 0–300 m.
Turn off the heat, uncover, wait 5 minutes and lift the jars onto a towel. Leave 12–24 hours, check the seals, and wipe the jars — beet juice stains.
recipes.keeps: 12–18 months in a cool dark cupboard. Refrigerate after opening and eat within a month.
recipes.variations: Pickled whole baby beets: use beets 2.5–4 cm (1–1½ inches) across and pack them whole instead of sliced, same brine and the same 30 minutes. Onions may be left out.

recipes.title: Home-style pickled jalapeños
recipes.tagline: Taqueria-style jalapeño strips with carrot and onion in a plain vinegar brine — the tested, lime-free way to put up a hot-pepper glut.
recipes.makes: About 6 × 500 ml (pint) jars
safety: Equal parts 5% vinegar and water is the tested brine for this quantity of peppers, carrot and onion — do not add more vegetables, more water or more garlic than the recipe gives.
Carrot, onion and garlic are low-acid; one crushed clove per jar and the amounts written are what was tested.
Peppers are raw-packed, so the brine must be boiling when it goes in and the jars go into a hot (not boiling) canner.
Gloves on, hands off faces, and wash the cutting board before the next job; capsaicin lingers.
The NCHFP recipe for true jalapeño rings uses an 18-hour lime soak for crispness, and its three rinse-and-soak cycles are what make it safe; this Ball recipe gets a similar jar without the lime.
ingredients: 1.6 kg (3½ lb) jalapeño peppers, seeded and quartered lengthwise
250 ml (1 cup) thinly sliced white onion
2 large carrots, thinly sliced
625 ml (2½ cups) white vinegar (5%)
625 ml (2½ cups) water
30 ml (2 tablespoons) pickling salt
15 ml (1 tablespoon) sugar
6 cloves garlic, crushed (1 per jar)
Calcium chloride (Pickle Crisp), optional: ⅛ teaspoon per jar
steps: Set 6 washed 500 ml jars to heat in simmering water in the canner — not boiling — and wash the lids. Put on gloves before touching a pepper; this is one recipe where the children slice carrots and onions and stay off the peppers.
Halve the jalapeños lengthwise, scrape out the seeds and membranes, then cut each half lengthwise again into long strips. Toss the strips with the onion and carrot in a big bowl.
Combine the vinegar, water, salt and sugar in a stainless steel or enamelled pot and bring to a boil.
Put 1 crushed garlic clove in a hot jar and pack it tightly with the pepper mixture, leaving 1.25 cm (½ inch) headspace. Add ⅛ teaspoon Pickle Crisp if you want them firmer.

Ladle the boiling liquid over the vegetables, keeping the 1.25 cm headspace and making sure everything is covered. Free bubbles with a chopstick, wipe the rim, centre the lid and screw the band on fingertip-tight. Repeat jar by jar.
Lower into the canner with at least 2.5 cm (1 inch) of water over the lids, bring to a full rolling boil and process 10 minutes at 0–300 m.
Turn off the heat, uncover, wait 5 minutes and lift the jars onto a towel. Leave 12–24 hours without tightening the bands, then check the seals.
recipes.keeps: 12 months in a cool dark cupboard. Refrigerate after opening and use within a month or two.
recipes.variations: Leave more membrane in for heat, or use a mix of red and green jalapeños late in the season for a prettier jar. The brine, vegetables and time stay the same.

recipes.title: Zucchini relish
recipes.tagline: Bernardin’s hot-dog relish for the zucchini that got away — a touch of horseradish and one hot pepper give it its bite.
recipes.makes: About 6 × 500 ml (pint) jars
recipes.total: Overnight salting plus 2½ hours, then 24 hours cooling
safety: Zucchini, onion and peppers are all low-acid; the 625 ml of 5% vinegar for these measured cups of vegetable is what makes the relish a boiling-water job. Measure the chopped vegetables, do not guess by weight alone.
Salt overnight, rinse and wring — the salting pulls water out so the vinegar is not diluted in the pot.
Boil it down until thick (about 45 minutes); a watery relish was not what was tested and separates in the jar.
No cornstarch or flour to thicken, and no extra vegetables. The horseradish is prepared (vinegar-packed) horseradish, not fresh grated root.
ingredients: 2 kg (4¼ lb) zucchini, about 14 medium — finely chopped to measure 3 L (12 cups)
675 g (1½ lb) onion, about 5 medium — finely chopped to measure 1 L (4 cups)
2 large sweet red peppers
1 large sweet green pepper
75 ml (⅓ cup) pickling salt
625 ml (2½ cups) granulated sugar
15 ml (1 tablespoon) each ground nutmeg and ground turmeric
625 ml (2½ cups) white vinegar (5%)
60 ml (4 tablespoons) prepared horseradish
1 large hot pepper, seeds and all, chopped
steps: The day before: pulse the zucchini in a food processor until finely chopped and measure 12 cups; do the same with the onions and measure 4 cups. Seed the sweet peppers, finely chop the green one and cut the red ones into 6 mm (¼ inch) cubes. Toss everything in a large glass or stainless bowl with the pickling salt, cover and refrigerate overnight.

Next day, tip the vegetables into a colander, rinse under cold running water, then line the colander with cheesecloth and twist the bundle hard to wring out as much water as you can — a satisfying job for strong small hands.

Put the vegetables in a large stainless steel pot with the sugar, nutmeg, turmeric, vinegar, horseradish and hot pepper. Bring to a boil, then lower the heat and boil gently, stirring often, until thick — about 45 minutes.
Meanwhile set 6 washed 500 ml jars on the rack in the canner, cover with water and heat to a simmer (82 °C / 180 °F). Wash the lids in hot soapy water and set them aside with the bands.

Ladle the hot relish into a hot jar to within 1 cm (½ inch) of the rim. Slide a plastic knife or chopstick around the inside to free bubbles, wipe the rim clean of any stickiness, centre the lid and screw the band down to fingertip-tight. Put the jar back in the canner and repeat.
With the jars covered by water, put the lid on the canner and bring it to a full boil. Process 15 minutes at 0–300 m.
Turn off the heat, lift the jars out without tilting and cool them upright, undisturbed, 24 hours. Do not retighten the bands. Check that every lid curves down; refrigerate any that did not seal.
recipes.keeps: 12–18 months in a cool dark cupboard. Refrigerate after opening and use within a month or two.
recipes.variations: Leave out the hot pepper for a mild relish children will eat on everything — the vinegar ratio does not change. Nutmeg is the flavour people either love or leave out; it can be dropped.

recipes.title: Green tomato salsa verde
recipes.tagline: The frost-night answer for a counter full of green tomatoes: a sharp, cumin-scented salsa verde in small jars.
recipes.makes: About 6 × 250 ml (half-pint) jars
safety: Measure everything in metric or everything in US cups — never mix the two, or the acid ratio shifts.
The 125 ml of bottled lime juice against 7 cups of green tomato and 2 cups of onion is the tested ratio; use bottled juice, never fresh, and never less.
Use between 5 and 10 hot peppers as written — never more than 10 — and do not add other vegetables; onion and garlic are already at their tested amounts.
Half-pint (250 ml) jars only — the 20 minutes was established for that size.
Green tomatoes from frost-killed plants are fine to eat but should not be canned; pick them before the frost.
Wear gloves for hot peppers and keep children away from the pepper board.
ingredients: 1.75 L (7 cups) chopped, cored, peeled green tomatoes — about 12 medium
5–10 jalapeño, habanero or Scotch bonnet peppers, seeded and finely chopped
500 ml (2 cups) chopped red onion — about 2 large
2 cloves garlic, finely chopped
125 ml (½ cup) bottled lime juice
125 ml (½ cup) loosely packed finely chopped cilantro
10 ml (2 teaspoons) ground cumin
5 ml (1 teaspoon) dried oregano
5 ml (1 teaspoon) salt
5 ml (1 teaspoon) freshly ground black pepper
steps: Set 6 washed 250 ml jars to heat in simmering water in the canner — do not boil them — and wash the lids in warm soapy water.

Wash the green tomatoes (a child’s job) and dip them in boiling water about a minute, then into cold water. Green skins do not always slip; peel with a paring knife where they cling. Core and chop, and measure 7 cups.
Gloves on for the peppers: stem, seed and finely chop as many as you want between 5 and 10. Chop the onion, garlic and cilantro.
Combine the tomatoes, peppers, onion, garlic and lime juice in a large pot and bring to a boil. Stir in the cilantro, cumin, oregano, salt and pepper, lower the heat and simmer 5 minutes.
Ladle the hot salsa into a hot jar, leaving 1.25 cm (½ inch) headspace. Free bubbles with a chopstick, wipe the rim, centre the lid and screw the band on fingertip-tight. Repeat.
Lower the jars into the canner with at least 2.5 cm (1 inch) of water over the lids, cover, bring to a full rolling boil and process 20 minutes at 0–300 m.
Turn off the heat, uncover and wait 5 minutes. Lift the jars onto a towel, leave 12–24 hours without touching the bands, and check the seals.
recipes.keeps: 12–18 months in a cool dark cupboard. Refrigerate after opening and use within a week.
recipes.variations: Five jalapeños makes a salsa most of the family can eat; ten habaneros is a different animal. The cilantro cooks out somewhat — add a fresh handful when you open a jar.

recipes.title: Pickled carrots
recipes.tagline: Sweet-sour carrot coins with mustard and celery seed — a bright lunchbox pickle from the roots that will not all fit in the cold room.
recipes.makes: About 4 × 500 ml (pint) jars
safety: Carrots are low-acid; this brine is unusually strong (5½ cups vinegar to 1 cup water) and that ratio is the whole safety case. Do not add water to soften it.
Half-cook the carrots in the brine (hot pack) — the tested 15 minutes assumes hot carrots going into the jar.
Pints only; no time was established for quarts.
Two headspaces: carrots to 2.5 cm from the rim, liquid to 1.25 cm. Carrots above the liquid darken and soften.
ingredients: 1.25 kg (2¾ lb) peeled carrots — about 1.6 kg (3½ lb) as pulled
1.375 L (5½ cups) white distilled vinegar (5%)
250 ml (1 cup) water
400 g (2 cups) sugar
10 ml (2 teaspoons) canning salt
40 ml (8 teaspoons) mustard seed — 2 teaspoons per jar
20 ml (4 teaspoons) celery seed — 1 teaspoon per jar

process.headspace: 1.25 cm (½ inch) of liquid over carrots packed to 2.5 cm (1 inch)

steps: Set 4 washed 500 ml jars to heat in the canner and wash the lids. Scrub, peel and wash the carrots again — a child can peel the fat ones — and cut them into rounds about 1.25 cm (½ inch) thick.
Combine the vinegar, water, sugar and salt in a large pot, bring to a boil and boil gently 3 minutes.
Add the carrots, bring back to a boil, then lower to a simmer until they are half-cooked, about 10 minutes.
Put 2 teaspoons mustard seed and 1 teaspoon celery seed in the bottom of each hot jar.

Fill the jars with hot carrots to 2.5 cm (1 inch) from the rim, then ladle in the hot liquid to 1.25 cm (½ inch) from the rim. Free bubbles with a chopstick and top up, wipe the rims with a damp paper towel, centre the lids and screw the bands on fingertip-tight.
Lower into the canner with at least 5 cm (2 inches) of water over the lids, bring to a full rolling boil and process 15 minutes at 0–300 m.
Turn off the heat, uncover, wait 5 minutes and lift the jars onto a towel. Leave 12–24 hours, check the seals, and wait 3–5 days before opening the first jar.
recipes.keeps: 12 months in a cool dark cupboard. Refrigerate after opening and eat within a month.
recipes.variations: Mixed orange, yellow and purple carrots make a jar worth giving away. For sticks rather than coins, keep them the same thickness and the same half-cooking time.

recipes.title: Applesauce, water-bath canned
recipes.tagline: Sound apples — seconds are fine once the bruises are cut away — into the easiest jar of the year; no added acid needed, and sugar optional.
recipes.makes: About 7 × 1 L (quart) jars from 9.5 kg (21 lb) of apples; 6.1 kg (13½ lb) fills 9 × 500 ml (pint) jars
safety: Apples are a high-acid fruit; no lemon juice or citric acid is needed for safety — the ascorbic acid is only for colour. That holds for fresh, firm apples with no rot or mould: cut out bruises, never use windfalls, and refrigerate or freeze sauce made from apples that have been stored a long time, which can be less acidic.
Hot pack only: the sauce must be boiling when it goes into the jars, which is why it is reheated after milling.
Sugar is for taste, not safety; leave it out entirely if you like.
Do not add butter, cream or thickeners — this is a plain fruit recipe. Cinnamon goes on at the table.
ingredients: 9.5 kg (21 lb) sweet, juicy, crisp apples — about 1.4 kg (3 lb) per litre jar; for a tart sauce, use 1–2 parts tart apples to 3 parts sweet
125 ml (½ cup) water for the pot
Ascorbic acid, optional, to stop browning: 1 teaspoon (3 g) in 4 L of cold water, or six crushed 500 mg vitamin C tablets
Sugar, optional: 30 ml (⅛ cup) per litre of sauce, or to taste
steps: Set the washed jars to heat in the canner and wash the lids. Wash, peel and core the apples; children can wash and feed the peeler. If it will be a while before they cook, drop the slices into the ascorbic-acid water.
Drain the slices into an 8–10 L pot, add the ½ cup of water and heat quickly, stirring now and then so nothing catches, until tender — 5–20 minutes depending on the variety.
Press through a food mill or sieve for a smooth sauce, or mash in the pot for a chunky one. Taste; stir in sugar if you want it (⅛ cup per litre is the starting point).
Bring the sauce back to a boil, stirring — it spits, so keep little helpers back.
Fill the hot jars with boiling sauce, leaving 1.25 cm (½ inch) headspace. Work a chopstick through to free trapped air, wipe the rims, centre the lids and screw the bands on fingertip-tight.
Lower into the canner with at least 5 cm (2 inches) of water over the lids, bring to a full rolling boil and time it: 500 ml jars 15 minutes, 1 L jars 20 minutes at 0–300 m.
Turn off the heat, uncover, wait 5 minutes, lift the jars onto a towel and leave 12–24 hours. Check the seals; refrigerate any that failed and eat within a week.
recipes.keeps: 12–18 months in a cool dark cupboard. Refrigerate after opening and eat within a week.
recipes.variations: Mixing varieties — a McIntosh for softness, a Cortland or Spartan for body, a crab or two for tang — gives the best sauce.

recipes.title: Apple butter, water-bath canned
recipes.tagline: A long, slow pot of apples, cider and spice cooked down to something that mounds on a spoon — the whole house smells of it.
recipes.makes: About 9–10 × 500 ml (pint) jars, or twice as many 250 ml
safety: Because 250 ml and 500 ml jars are processed only 5 minutes, they must be sterilized in boiling water for 10 minutes before filling. Quart jars get 10 minutes in the canner and skip the pre-boil.
The cider and vinegar are part of the tested recipe; the vinegar sharpens and acidifies, so do not leave it out or swap it for water.
Cook until it truly mounds — a thin butter weeps and was not what was tested.
Headspace is a tight 6 mm (¼ inch).
ingredients: 3.6 kg (8 lb) tasty apples — McIntosh, Golden Delicious, Cortland, Jonagold or a mix
500 ml (2 cups) apple cider (sweet, unfermented)
500 ml (2 cups) vinegar (5%) — cider vinegar is traditional
450 g (2¼ cups) white sugar
500 g (2¼ cups, packed) brown sugar
30 ml (2 tablespoons) ground cinnamon
15 ml (1 tablespoon) ground cloves

process.jars: 250 ml (half-pint) or 500 ml (pint) · 1 L (quart) in brackets

steps: Wash the apples, pull the stems, quarter and core them — no need to peel. Put them in a large heavy pot with the cider and vinegar and cook slowly until soft.
Press the fruit through a food mill, colander or strainer to leave the skins behind. A child can turn the food-mill handle.
Return the pulp to the pot with both sugars and the spices. Cook slowly, stirring often and more often as it thickens — it spits, so a long spoon and a splatter screen help. Expect 1–2 hours.

Test for doneness: lift a spoonful, hold it away from the steam 2 minutes, and see if it stays mounded on the spoon. Or spoon a little onto a plate — when no ring of liquid separates around the edge, it is ready.

Sterilize the jars while the butter finishes, because the process is under 10 minutes: boil the empty 250 ml or 500 ml jars, covered by water, 10 minutes (one minute more per 300 m above sea level) and keep them in the hot water. Wash the lids.
Fill the hot jars with boiling-hot butter, leaving 6 mm (¼ inch) headspace. Free bubbles, wipe the rims, centre the lids and screw the bands on fingertip-tight.

Lower into the canner with at least 5 cm (2 inches) of water over the lids, bring to a full rolling boil and process 250 ml or 500 ml jars 5 minutes at 0–300 m (1 L jars, which need not be sterilized: 10 minutes).
Turn off the heat, uncover, wait 5 minutes and lift the jars onto a towel. Leave 12–24 hours, check the seals and store.
recipes.keeps: 12–18 months in a cool dark cupboard. Refrigerate after opening and use within a month.
recipes.variations: A slow cooker on low, lid ajar, will do the long reduction overnight — not part of the tested method, so the mound test still decides doneness, and the butter comes to a full boil on the stove before filling the jars. The NCHFP also publishes a reduced-sugar apple butter with its own method.

recipes.title: Pear halves in light syrup or juice
recipes.tagline: Bartletts picked hard and ripened in a box, then put up in a light syrup or plain apple juice — winter dessert on a shelf.
recipes.makes: About 7 × 1 L (quart) jars from 8 kg (17½ lb) of pears; 5 kg (11 lb) fills 9 × 500 ml (pint) jars
safety: Pears are acidic enough on their own; the syrup is for flavour, colour and shape, not safety, so a very light syrup or plain juice is just as safe as a heavy one.
Hot pack only — 5 minutes boiling in the liquid before filling — and the processing time assumes it.
Use ripe, sound fruit; cut away bruises generously and leave out anything soft or fermenting.
Boiling-water processing is the better choice for pears; the source notes that pressure canning can turn them pink.
ingredients: 8 kg (17½ lb) ripe but firm pears — about 1.1 kg (2½ lb) per litre jar
Anti-browning bath: 1 teaspoon (3 g) ascorbic acid, or six crushed 500 mg vitamin C tablets, in 4 L (1 US gallon) cold water
Light syrup for a 7-quart load: 2.25 L (9 cups) water with 450 g (2¼ cups) sugar — for 9 pints, 1.45 L (5¾ cups) water with 300 g (1½ cups) sugar
Very light syrup instead, if you prefer: 2.6 L (10½ cups) water with 250 g (1¼ cups) sugar for 7 quarts — or skip syrup and use plain apple juice, white grape juice or water

process.altitude: 1 L jars: 25 min. For both sizes add 5 min at 300–900 m (1,001–3,000 ft), 10 min at 900–1,800 m (3,001–6,000 ft), 15 min above 1,800 m (6,000 ft).

steps: Set the washed jars to heat in the canner and wash the lids. Mix the ascorbic-acid bath in a big bowl.

Wash and peel the pears, halve them lengthwise and scoop out the core with a melon baller or a metal measuring spoon — children manage the scooping once an adult has halved. Drop the halves straight into the ascorbic-acid water.
Heat the water and sugar for the syrup (or the juice) to a boil in a wide pot.
Drain the pears and boil them 5 minutes in the syrup or juice. Raw-packed pears turn out poorly, so do not skip this.

Fill the hot jars with the hot pear halves, cut side down and overlapping, and cover with the hot cooking liquid, leaving 1.25 cm (½ inch) headspace. Free bubbles with a chopstick, top up, wipe the rims, centre the lids and screw the bands on fingertip-tight.
Lower into the canner with at least 5 cm (2 inches) of water over the lids, bring to a full rolling boil and time it: 500 ml jars 20 minutes, 1 L jars 25 minutes at 0–300 m.
Turn off the heat, uncover, wait 5 minutes, lift the jars onto a towel and leave 12–24 hours. Check the seals; refrigerate any that failed and eat within a few days.
recipes.keeps: 12–18 months in a cool dark cupboard. Refrigerate after opening and eat within 3–4 days.
recipes.variations: A vanilla bean or a strip of lemon zest in the syrup is a flavouring, not a vegetable, and is fine. Asian pears are a different fruit with their own NCHFP recipe that requires added lemon juice — do not use these times for them.

recipes.title: Refrigerator pickled garlic (garlic in vinegar)
recipes.tagline: Whole peeled cloves kept under full-strength vinegar in the fridge — the safe way to have mellow pickled garlic through the winter without a canner.
recipes.makes: A 250 ml (half-pint) jar holds about 2 heads of garlic (around 25 cloves); scale up jar by jar
recipes.total: 20 minutes, then 1–2 weeks in the fridge before eating
safety: This is a refrigerator pickle, not a canned one: garlic is a low-acid vegetable and there is no tested boiling-water time for plain garlic on any of the public canning sites. It stays cold from the day it is made.
Undiluted vinegar or wine only. Diluting it with water or oil raises the pH and makes the jar unsafe.
Never put raw garlic in oil at room temperature — garlic in oil has caused botulism outbreaks. Garlic in oil belongs in the freezer, or in the fridge for no more than 4 days.
Keep every clove under the liquid. Throw out the jar — cloves and liquid — at the first sign of mould or yeast on the surface.
Cloves that turn blue or green in vinegar are safe; the pigment reaction is cosmetic and more common with immature garlic.

source.label: UC ANR 8568: Garlic — Safe Methods to Store, Preserve, and Enjoy (storing garlic in wine or vinegar)

ingredients: Firm, cured garlic cloves, peeled and left whole — about 2 heads (100 g) per 250 ml jar
Undiluted (full-strength) vinegar to cover — white or wine vinegar, 5% acidity; roughly 200 ml per 250 ml jar — or a dry white or red wine instead
Optional: a few whole peppercorns, a pinch of chili flakes or cumin seed, or a bay leaf
steps: Break the heads into cloves and peel them — a job children do happily if you crack the skins first by pressing each clove under the flat of a knife. Discard any soft, sprouting or bruised cloves.
Pack the whole cloves into a clean 250 ml jar with the spices, if using, leaving room so the liquid can cover them completely.
Pour in full-strength vinegar (or wine) until every clove is submerged, with a little to spare. Do not dilute it with water.
Put the lid on, write the date and a ‘best before’ four months on, and put the jar straight in the refrigerator — never on the counter.
Wait a week or two for the raw bite to soften. Eat the cloves as a pickle, chop them into dressings, and use the garlicky vinegar in vinaigrettes.
recipes.keeps: About 4 months in the refrigerator — label the jar. Longer is not unsafe in itself, but mould becomes likely and the flavour fades.
recipes.variations: A mix of white vinegar and dry white wine is pleasant; so is a jar of cloves in red wine vinegar with a pinch of dried rosemary (dried spices only — fresh herbs are not in the tested method). Oregon State’s garlic page gives the same method and the same rules.

recipes.title: Green beans, pressure canned
recipes.tagline: The first thing most people pressure-can, and the jar that teaches the whole method: plain beans, salt if you like, nothing else.
recipes.makes: About 9 × 500 ml (pint) jars from 4 kg (9 lb) of beans, or 7 × 1 L (quart) jars from 6.4 kg (14 lb)
recipes.total: 2½ hours including venting, processing and cooling the canner
safety: Green beans are a low-acid vegetable and can only be canned in a pressure canner. A boiling-water bath, however long, does not reach the 116 °C (240 °F) needed to kill Clostridium botulinum spores.
Do not add bacon, onion, butter or tomatoes — those are different recipes with their own tested times, or no tested time at all.
Vent the canner for 10 minutes before pressurising; trapped air makes the inside cooler than the gauge says.
If a jar has lost a lot of liquid, that is a quality issue, not a safety one, as long as it sealed and was processed the full time. Use it first.

Know your altitude. Much of southern Quebec and Ontario sits under 300 m, but the Laurentians, Eastern Townships and Gatineau Hills climb above it, and the weighted gauge jumps to 15 psi the moment you do.

source.label: NCHFP: Beans, snap and Italian — pieces (green and wax)

ingredients: 6.4 kg (14 lb) young, tender green or wax beans for 7 L jars — 4 kg (9 lb) for 9 × 500 ml jars
Canning or pickling salt, optional: 1 teaspoon (5 ml) per 1 L jar, ½ teaspoon per 500 ml jar — flavour only
Boiling water to cover

process.altitude: 1 L jars: 25 min. Weighted gauge: 10 psi at 0–300 m (0–1,000 ft), 15 psi above 300 m. Dial gauge: 11 psi at 0–600 m (0–2,000 ft), 12 psi at 600–1,200 m, 13 psi at 1,200–1,800 m, 14 psi at 1,800–2,400 m. Processing time does not change with altitude for pressure canning — only the pressure does.

steps: Put 5–7.5 cm (2–3 inches) of water in the pressure canner and set it to heat. Wash the jars and keep them hot; wash the lids in hot soapy water and set them aside.
Rinse the beans and snap off both ends. Leave whole or snap into 2.5 cm (1 inch) pieces — this is the job for small hands, and a child can fill a bowl while you fill the canner.
Hot pack (best texture): drop the beans into boiling water, bring back to the boil and boil 5 minutes. Raw pack: skip the boil and pack the raw beans tightly instead.

Fill the hot jars — loosely for hot pack, tightly for raw — leaving 2.5 cm (1 inch) headspace. Add salt if using. Cover with the hot cooking liquid (or boiling water for raw pack), keeping that 2.5 cm headspace.
Run a chopstick or bubble tool around the inside to free trapped air, top up if needed, wipe the rims, centre the lids and screw the bands on fingertip-tight. Lower the jars onto the rack.

Lock the lid, leave the weight off the vent and heat on high until steam streams steadily out. Let it vent for a full 10 minutes, then put the weight on (or close the petcock) and bring to pressure: 10 psi weighted or 11 psi dial at 0–300 m.

Start timing when the weight begins to rock or the dial reaches pressure: 500 ml jars 20 minutes, 1 L jars 25 minutes. Adjust the heat to hold the pressure steady; if it ever drops below target, bring it back and start the full time again.

Turn off the heat and let the canner cool on its own — never run water over it or lift the weight early. When the gauge reads zero (or the lock drops), remove the weight, wait 10 minutes, then open the lid away from your face.
Lift the jars straight up onto a towel and leave them 12–24 hours. Press each lid: a sealed one is dished and does not move. Refrigerate any that did not seal and eat within a few days.
recipes.keeps: Best within 12 months in a cool dark cupboard, safe longer if the seal holds. Refrigerate after opening and use within 3–4 days. Never taste a jar that has lost its seal, bulges, leaks, spurts or smells off: treat it as containing botulinum toxin and dispose of it following NCHFP’s steps for spoiled canned food.
recipes.variations: Wax beans and flat Italian (Romano) beans use the same times. Mixed-colour jars are pretty on the shelf and taste the same.

recipes.title: Carrots, pressure canned
recipes.tagline: For the carrots that will not fit in the cold room: sweet, soft, and ready for soup, stew or a toddler’s plate in a minute.
recipes.makes: About 9 × 500 ml (pint) jars from 5 kg (11 lb) of topped carrots, or 7 × 1 L (quart) jars from 8 kg (17½ lb)
recipes.total: 2½ hours including venting, processing and cooling the canner
safety: Carrots are low-acid: pressure canner only. The same times cover hot and raw pack, and they do not shorten for small dice.
Do not pack in a sugar glaze, butter or stock — plain water or the cooking water only.
Big woody carrots make a fibrous jar; it is a quality problem, not a safety one, but it is why the recipe asks for small ones.
Never leave the weight off to speed things up, and never cool the canner under the tap — a sudden pressure drop siphons liquid out of the jars and can break them.
ingredients: 8 kg (17½ lb) carrots without tops for 7 L jars — 5 kg (11 lb) for 9 × 500 ml jars; small young carrots give the best jar
Canning or pickling salt, optional: 1 teaspoon (5 ml) per 1 L jar, ½ teaspoon per 500 ml jar
Boiling water to cover

process.altitude: 1 L jars: 30 min. Weighted gauge: 10 psi at 0–300 m (0–1,000 ft), 15 psi above 300 m. Dial gauge: 11 psi at 0–600 m (0–2,000 ft), 12 psi at 600–1,200 m, 13 psi at 1,200–1,800 m, 14 psi at 1,800–2,400 m. Processing time does not change with altitude for pressure canning — only the pressure does.

steps: Put 5–7.5 cm (2–3 inches) of water in the pressure canner and start heating it. Wash the jars and keep them hot; wash the lids and set them aside.
Scrub, peel and rinse the carrots again, then slice into coins or dice. A child with a crinkle cutter can do the slicing once the carrots are peeled.
Hot pack: put the carrots in a pot, cover with boiling water, bring to the boil and simmer 5 minutes. Raw pack: fill the jars tightly with raw slices instead.
Fill the hot jars leaving 2.5 cm (1 inch) headspace. Add salt if using. Cover with the hot cooking liquid or boiling water, keeping the 2.5 cm headspace.
Free the air bubbles with a chopstick, adjust the liquid, wipe the rims, fit the lids and bands fingertip-tight, and set the jars on the rack.
Lock the lid and let steam vent hard for 10 minutes before adding the weight. Bring to 10 psi (weighted) or 11 psi (dial) at 0–300 m.
Time from the moment the weight rocks or the dial reads pressure: 500 ml jars 25 minutes, 1 L jars 30 minutes. If the pressure drops, bring it back and restart the clock.
Let the canner cool naturally to zero, remove the weight, wait 10 minutes, open the lid away from you and lift the jars onto a towel. Leave 12–24 hours, then check the seals and remove the bands.
recipes.keeps: Best within 12 months in a cool dark cupboard. Refrigerate after opening and use within 3–4 days.
recipes.variations: Mixing carrots with other vegetables changes the recipe; follow NCHFP’s mixed-vegetables page (longer times) rather than this one.

recipes.title: Potatoes, cubed and pressure canned
recipes.tagline: Hot-packed cubes that go straight from jar to frying pan: the fastest home-fries you will ever make, from the potatoes that would not keep.
recipes.makes: About 9 × 500 ml (pint) jars from 6 kg (13 lb) of potatoes, or 7 × 1 L (quart) jars from 9 kg (20 lb)
recipes.total: 3 hours including venting, processing and cooling the canner
safety: Potatoes are low-acid and dense: pressure canner only, hot pack only. There is no tested raw-pack time, so do not pack them raw.
Cubes must be 1.25 cm (½ inch) or whole potatoes under 5 cm (2 inches) across — bigger pieces heat too slowly for the tested time.
Cover with fresh boiling water. The cooking water is thick with starch and slows heat penetration.
No butter, milk, cream or mashing — mashed potatoes cannot be safely canned at home.

source.label: NCHFP: Potatoes, white — cubed or whole

ingredients: 9 kg (20 lb) small to medium mature potatoes for 7 L jars — 6 kg (13 lb) for 9 × 500 ml jars
Anti-browning soak: 1 teaspoon (3 g) ascorbic acid stirred into 4 L (1 gallon) cold water
Canning or pickling salt, optional: 1 teaspoon (5 ml) per 1 L jar, ½ teaspoon per 500 ml jar
Fresh boiling water to cover — not the cooking water

process.altitude: 1 L jars: 40 min. Weighted gauge: 10 psi at 0–300 m (0–1,000 ft), 15 psi above 300 m. Dial gauge: 11 psi at 0–600 m (0–2,000 ft), 12 psi at 600–1,200 m, 13 psi at 1,200–1,800 m, 14 psi at 1,800–2,400 m. Processing time does not change with altitude for pressure canning — only the pressure does.

steps: Set the pressure canner heating with 5–7.5 cm (2–3 inches) of water. Wash the jars and keep them hot; wash the lids and set aside.

Wash and peel the potatoes, cutting away any eyes, green patches or bruises. Cut into 1.25 cm (½ inch) cubes and drop them straight into the ascorbic-acid water so they do not brown. A child can do the dropping — and count the cubes.
Drain the cubes, cover with fresh water in a big pot, bring to the boil and boil 2 minutes (whole small potatoes 2.5–5 cm across get 10 minutes). Drain.
Fill the hot jars with the hot cubes, leaving 2.5 cm (1 inch) headspace. Add salt if using.
Cover with fresh boiling water, not the starchy cooking water, keeping 2.5 cm headspace. Free the bubbles, wipe the rims, fit the lids fingertip-tight and load the canner.
Lock the lid, vent steam for 10 minutes, then weight the vent and bring to 10 psi weighted or 11 psi dial at 0–300 m.
Time once at pressure: 500 ml jars 35 minutes, 1 L jars 40 minutes. Hold the pressure steady; if it drops, bring it back and start over.
Cool the canner naturally to zero, remove the weight, wait 10 minutes, open away from your face, and lift the jars onto a towel for 12–24 hours. Check the seals and label.
recipes.keeps: Best within 12 months. Drain and rinse before frying or roasting. Refrigerate after opening and use within 3–4 days.
recipes.variations: Whole new potatoes no bigger than 5 cm across use the same times with a 10-minute pre-boil. Potatoes that have been stored cold may darken in the jar — harmless, but a reason to can from fresh-dug stock.

recipes.title: Pumpkin and winter squash cubes, pressure canned
recipes.tagline: The only safe way to put squash in a jar: firm cubes in water, which you drain and mash the day you bake the pie.
recipes.makes: About 9 × 500 ml (pint) jars from 4.5 kg (10 lb) of squash, or 7 × 1 L (quart) jars from 7.3 kg (16 lb)
recipes.total: 3½ hours including venting, processing and cooling the canner
safety: Purée cannot be canned at home, full stop. Mashed pumpkin is so thick that heat crawls to the centre of the jar unevenly, and tests at the University of Minnesota found batch-to-batch thickness varied too much for any single time to cover. No research has established a safe home-canning time, so none exists — for purée, pumpkin butter or pie filling.
Cubes only, 2.5 cm (1 inch), boiled just 2 minutes so they stay firm and the water can move between them.
Pressure canner only; this is a low-acid vegetable, and adding sugar, vinegar or lemon does not change that.
Mash after you open the jar: drain the cubes, press through a sieve or mash, and use as you would canned pumpkin.
For a smooth product that keeps, freeze it instead — see frozen squash purée.

source.label: NCHFP: Pumpkins and winter squash — cubed

ingredients: 7.3 kg (16 lb) hard-rinded pumpkin or winter squash for 7 L jars — 4.5 kg (10 lb) for 9 × 500 ml jars; about 1 kg (2¼ lb) per litre jar. Pie pumpkins, butternut and buttercup work better than jack-o’-lantern types
Water for boiling and covering

process.altitude: 1 L jars: 90 min. Weighted gauge: 10 psi at 0–300 m (0–1,000 ft), 15 psi above 300 m. Dial gauge: 11 psi at 0–600 m (0–2,000 ft), 12 psi at 600–1,200 m, 13 psi at 1,200–1,800 m, 14 psi at 1,800–2,400 m. Processing time does not change with altitude for pressure canning — only the pressure does.

steps: Start the pressure canner heating with 5–7.5 cm (2–3 inches) of water. Wash the jars and keep them hot.
Wash the squash, split it and scoop out the seeds (save them to roast — a child’s job). Cut into 2.5 cm (1 inch) wide slices, peel each slice, then cut into 2.5 cm (1 inch) cubes.
Put the cubes in a pot, cover with water, bring to the boil and boil 2 minutes. Do not cook them soft and do not mash.
Fill the hot jars with the cubes and the cooking liquid, leaving 2.5 cm (1 inch) headspace. The cubes should stay whole and swim in liquid.
Free the air bubbles, wipe the rims, centre the lids and tighten the bands fingertip-tight. Set the jars on the rack.
Lock the lid, vent steam for 10 minutes, then weight the vent and bring to 10 psi weighted or 11 psi dial at 0–300 m.
Time once at pressure: 500 ml jars 55 minutes, 1 L jars 90 minutes. Keep the pressure steady; if it falls below target, bring it back and start the full time again.
Cool the canner naturally to zero, remove the weight, wait 10 minutes, open the lid away from you and lift the jars onto a towel. Leave 12–24 hours before checking seals.
recipes.keeps: Best within 12 months. Drain and mash on the day you use it. Refrigerate after opening and use within 3–4 days.
recipes.variations: Any hard winter squash — butternut, buttercup, hubbard, kabocha — cans the same way. Spaghetti squash is a poor choice because it falls into strands.

recipes.title: Dry beans, soaked and pressure canned
recipes.tagline: Your own shelled beans — or a 10 kg sack from the store — turned into ready-to-eat jars without the overnight planning every single time.
recipes.makes: About 9 × 500 ml (pint) jars from 1.5 kg (3¼ lb) of dry beans, or 7 × 1 L (quart) jars from 2.3 kg (5 lb)
recipes.total: Overnight soak, then about 3½ hours including the 30-minute boil, processing and cooling
safety: Beans must be soaked and boiled 30 minutes before they go in the jar. Dry beans packed raw with water — the so-called dry-canning shortcut — do not heat through and have no tested time.
Leave the full 2.5 cm (1 inch) headspace; beans swell and a jar packed to the brim will siphon and may not seal.
Pressure canner only, 75/90 minutes. These are among the longest home-canning times for a reason: a jar of beans is dense.
Plain beans in water only. Tomato sauce, molasses, pork and seasonings belong to NCHFP’s separate baked-bean recipes with their own times.

source.label: NCHFP: Beans or peas — shelled, dried, all varieties

ingredients: 2.3 kg (5 lb) dry beans or peas of one kind — kidney, pinto, black, navy, cranberry, chickpea — for 7 L jars; 1.5 kg (3¼ lb) for 9 × 500 ml jars
Water for soaking and boiling
Canning or pickling salt, optional: 1 teaspoon (5 ml) per 1 L jar, ½ teaspoon per 500 ml jar

process.altitude: 1 L jars: 90 min. Weighted gauge: 10 psi at 0–300 m (0–1,000 ft), 15 psi above 300 m. Dial gauge: 11 psi at 0–600 m (0–2,000 ft), 12 psi at 600–1,200 m, 13 psi at 1,200–1,800 m, 14 psi at 1,800–2,400 m. Processing time does not change with altitude for pressure canning — only the pressure does.

steps: Sort through the beans and throw out stones and shrivelled ones — a job a child can do on a tray. Rinse.

Soak one of two ways. Long soak: cover with plenty of cold water and leave 12–18 hours somewhere cool, then drain. Quick soak: cover with boiling water, boil 2 minutes, take off the heat, leave 1 hour, drain.
Set the pressure canner heating with 5–7.5 cm (2–3 inches) of water, and keep the washed jars hot.
Cover the drained beans with fresh water, bring to the boil and boil 30 minutes. They will still be firm; the canner finishes the cooking.
Add salt to the hot jars if using. Fill with beans and their cooking liquid, leaving 2.5 cm (1 inch) headspace — the beans keep swelling, so do not pack them tight.
Free the bubbles, wipe the rims, fit the lids fingertip-tight and load the canner. Lock the lid, vent steam for 10 minutes, then bring to 10 psi weighted or 11 psi dial at 0–300 m.
Time once at pressure: 500 ml jars 75 minutes, 1 L jars 90 minutes. Hold the pressure; if it drops, bring it back and restart the clock.
Cool the canner naturally to zero, remove the weight, wait 10 minutes, open away from your face, lift the jars onto a towel, and leave 12–24 hours before checking the seals.
recipes.keeps: Best within 12 months. Drain and rinse for salads; use the liquid in soups. Refrigerate after opening and use within 3–4 days.
recipes.variations: Any whole dry bean or whole dry pea (kidney, pinto, black, navy, cranberry, chickpea, black-eyed pea) uses the same method and times. Do not use it for split peas or red or split lentils, which cook down to a purée no tested time covers. Jars of black beans and chickpeas are the ones that disappear fastest.

recipes.title: Sauerkraut, crock or jar fermented
recipes.tagline: Cabbage, salt and three weeks of patience. The oldest recipe in this library, and the one a six-year-old can make almost entirely alone.
recipes.makes: About 2 L from a 2.3 kg (5 lb) batch in a 4 L jar; 9 L from 11 kg (25 lb) in a 20 L crock
safety: The salt is the recipe: 3 tablespoons per 2.3 kg (about 2.25% by weight). It is what lets the lactic-acid bacteria win and keeps the texture crisp. Do not cut it, and do not use iodized table salt, which clouds the brine.
Everything must stay under the brine. Cabbage in the air is where mould starts.
Surface scum is yeast and comes off with a spoon; coloured fuzzy mould, slime or an off smell means discard the batch.

Fermented kraut is a high-acid food, which is why it can be water-bath canned — but only with the tested times, and canning stops the live culture. Refrigerated kraut keeps its crunch and its bacteria.
Kraut that never got sour (too cold, too little salt) is not safe to can or keep. If it does not taste properly tangy after six weeks, compost it.
ingredients: 2.3 kg (5 lb) firm, fresh cabbage per 4 L (1 gallon) of container — scale up by the same ratio
3 tablespoons (45 ml, about 50 g) canning or pickling salt per 2.3 kg cabbage — about 2.25% by weight; if you have a scale, 22 g per kilogram of shredded cabbage
Top-up brine only if needed: 1½ tablespoons (22 ml) canning salt per 950 ml (1 quart) water, boiled and cooled

process.jars: 500 ml (pint) hot pack · 1 L (quart) in brackets
process.altitude: Hot pack 1 L jars: 15 min. Raw pack: 500 ml 20 min, 1 L 25 min. At 305–915 m (1,001–3,000 ft) hot pack is 15/20 min and raw pack 25/30 min; at 915–1,830 m (3,001–6,000 ft) hot pack 15/20 min and raw pack 30/35 min; above 1,830 m hot pack 20/25 min and raw pack 35/40 min.

steps: Pull off the loose outer leaves, rinse the heads, quarter them and cut out the cores. Shred to about the thickness of a quarter (about 2 mm) with a knife, mandoline or food processor.

Weigh the shredded cabbage into a big bowl, add the salt, and mix and squeeze with clean hands for several minutes until the cabbage goes limp and glossy and juice gathers in the bottom. Children love this step; the bowl can go on the floor.

Pack the cabbage into a clean 4 L jar or crock a handful at a time, pressing down hard with a fist or a wooden spoon so the juice rises above it. Leave at least 10–12 cm (4–5 inches) of space at the top.

If after an hour the juice does not cover the cabbage, top up with the cooled brine. Lay a plate or lid that fits inside the container on top, and weight it with a sealed jar of water or a brine-filled bag so everything stays 2.5–5 cm (1–2 inches) under the liquid. Cover with a clean tea towel.
Leave it somewhere 21–24 °C (70–75 °F) and it will finish in 3–4 weeks; at 15–18 °C (60–65 °F) allow 5–6 weeks. Below 15 °C it may not ferment at all; above 24 °C the kraut goes soft.

Look in two or three times a week. A white film or bubbly scum on the surface is wild yeast and is normal — skim it off, rinse the plate and weight, and put them back. Fuzzy, coloured mould, a slimy texture or a bad smell means the batch is finished, in the bin.
It is done when the bubbling stops and it tastes clean and sour all the way through. Put the whole container, covered, in the fridge, or pack into jars and refrigerate.

To can instead (optional): for a hot pack, bring the kraut and its juice to a boil, stirring, and fill hot jars firmly with 1.25 cm (½ inch) headspace; for a raw pack, fill cold jars firmly and cover with juice to the same headspace. Process in a boiling-water canner: hot pack 500 ml jars 10 minutes and 1 L jars 15 minutes; raw pack 500 ml 20 minutes and 1 L 25 minutes, at 0–300 m. Cool 12–24 hours and check the seals.
recipes.keeps: Tightly covered in the fridge, several months — it slowly gets more sour. Canned, best within a year in a cool dark cupboard; refrigerate after opening.
recipes.variations: A tablespoon of caraway or juniper per 2.3 kg goes in with the salt. A quarter of the cabbage swapped for shredded carrot or apple, with the salt kept at the same percentage of the total weight, makes a good fridge kraut — but mixed krauts are not the tested recipe, so keep them in the fridge and do not can them. Red cabbage makes a magenta kraut that stains everything cheerfully.

recipes.title: Brine-fermented dill pickles
recipes.tagline: Real deli pickles: cucumbers, dill, garlic and a salt brine, soured by the same bacteria that make kraut. No vinegar bite, just depth.
recipes.makes: About 2 × 1 L jars of pickles per 4 L (1 gallon) crock
safety: The brine as mixed is strong — 125 ml salt to 2 L water works out near 7% — because the cucumbers are mostly water and dilute it as they ferment to somewhere around 4%. That is why you cannot cut the salt and why the cucumber weight per container matters.
Canning or pickling salt only; iodized or anti-caking salt clouds the brine and can slow the ferment.
Keep everything under the brine and skim scum as soon as you see it. Soft, slimy or foul-smelling pickles are spoiled — do not can or eat them.
The 5% vinegar is part of the tested recipe; it gives the ferment a safe start. Do not leave it out.
Use the tested canning times only on properly soured pickles. Half-fermented cucumbers are not acidic enough for a water bath.
ingredients: 1.8 kg (4 lb) pickling cucumbers about 10 cm (4 inches) long, per 4 L (1 gallon) of container
2 tablespoons (30 ml) dill seed, or 4–5 heads of fresh or dried dill
125 ml (½ cup) canning or pickling salt
60 ml (¼ cup) vinegar, 5% acidity
2 L (8 cups) water
Optional: 2 cloves garlic, 2 dried hot red peppers, 2 teaspoons (10 ml) whole mixed pickling spice

process.altitude: 1 L jars: 15 min. At 305–1,830 m (1,001–6,000 ft): 500 ml 15 min, 1 L 20 min. Above 1,830 m: 500 ml 20 min, 1 L 25 min. Alternative that keeps them crisper: low-temperature pasteurization — jars in water at 49–60 °C, then heat to 82–85 °C (180–185 °F) and hold exactly 30 minutes with a thermometer, never hotter.

steps: Pick or buy cucumbers no more than a day old; limp ones make hollow pickles. Scrub them gently and cut a thin slice (about 2 mm, 1/16 inch) off the blossom end — it carries an enzyme that softens pickles. Leave a stub of stem.

Put half the dill and spices (and garlic and peppers, if using) in the bottom of a scrubbed 4 L crock, food-grade bucket or wide glass jar. A child can hand you the cucumbers to stand upright and pack snugly, then add the rest of the dill and spice on top.
Stir the salt into the water and vinegar until it dissolves, and pour it over the cucumbers so they are covered.
Set a plate that fits inside the container on top and weight it with a sealed jar of water so the cucumbers stay 2.5–5 cm (1–2 inches) under the brine. Cover with a clean tea towel.
Keep the container at 21–24 °C (70–75 °F) for about 3–4 weeks. At 13–18 °C (55–65 °F) it takes 5–6 weeks. Avoid anything above 27 °C (80 °F) — the pickles soften and spoil.

Look in several times a week and skim any white film or scum off the surface at once; rinse the plate and weight before putting them back. If the pickles go soft, slimy or smell bad, throw the batch out.
They are done when the bubbling has stopped and a pickle cut in half is the same translucent olive colour all the way through, with no white core. Taste one.

For the fridge: leave them in their brine, covered, and keep skimming. To can: pour the brine into a pot, bring to a boil and simmer 5 minutes, straining through coffee filters if you want it clear. Pack the pickles into hot jars, cover with the hot brine leaving 1.25 cm (½ inch) headspace, free the bubbles, wipe the rims and fit the lids fingertip-tight. Process in a boiling-water canner: 500 ml jars 10 minutes, 1 L jars 15 minutes at 0–300 m. Cool 12–24 hours and check the seals.
recipes.keeps: In the fridge in their brine, 4–6 months, as long as you keep skimming the surface. Canned, best within a year; refrigerate after opening.
recipes.variations: A few grape, oak, horseradish or black-currant leaves in the crock add tannin and help with crunch.

recipes.title: Fermented hot sauce (refrigerator only)
recipes.tagline: Brined peppers, soured for a few weeks and blended: the sauce every pepper-grower ends up making. Ours stays in the fridge, because nobody has published a tested canning time for it.
recipes.makes: About 500 ml of sauce from 500 g of peppers
safety: This is a refrigerator recipe. No university or Bernardin lab has published a tested water-bath time for home fermented hot sauce, and a blended sauce is thick enough that heat penetration cannot be guessed. Do not can it.
The brine is 5% by weight (50 g salt per litre of water). Weigh the salt; spoon measures vary between salt brands.
Peppers must stay under the brine. Anything poking into the air grows mould.
The vinegar at the end is for flavour and extra margin. Keep it in the fridge and use it within a few months; anything soft, slimy, pink or mouldy is finished.
Wear gloves, do not touch your face, and run the blender outdoors or under the range hood — the fumes from a litre of blended habaneros will clear a kitchen.

source.label: No tested home-canning recipe exists. Temperature, scum handling and spoilage signs follow NCHFP’s fermented dill pickles; the 5% brine is not from a tested source. Refrigerator only.

ingredients: 500 g (1 lb) hot peppers of any kind — jalapeño, cayenne, Hungarian wax, habanero, or a mix with some sweet red pepper to tame it
2–4 cloves garlic, optional
Brine: 50 g (about 3 tablespoons) canning or pickling salt dissolved in 1 L (4 cups) water — a 5% brine; use the full amount even if you do not need it all
60–125 ml (¼–½ cup) vinegar, 5% acidity, to finish
steps: Put on gloves — the capsaicin lingers on skin for hours — and keep children well back from the cutting board for this one; they can take over at the blending stage. Wash the peppers, pull off the stems, and halve or slice them. Leave the seeds in for more heat or scrape them out.
Pack the peppers and garlic into a clean 1 L glass jar, stopping 5 cm (2 inches) from the top.
Stir the salt into the water until it dissolves completely and pour the brine over the peppers to cover them. Save the rest of the brine in the fridge for topping up.

Hold the peppers under the brine with a small jar, a fermentation weight or a zip bag filled with the spare brine. Cover the jar loosely — a lid left a quarter-turn open, or a fermentation airlock — so gas can escape.

Leave it at 21–24 °C (70–75 °F), out of direct sun. It will fizz within a few days and smell sharp and pleasant. Check every day or two: top up with brine if the level drops and skim any white film at once. Fuzzy or coloured mould, slime or a rotten smell means discard it.

After 2 weeks (up to 4 for a deeper flavour) the bubbling slows and the brine tastes clearly sour. Pour off and keep the brine, tip the peppers and garlic into a blender, and blend smooth with the vinegar and as much brine as you need for a pourable sauce.
Strain through a sieve for a thin sauce or leave it thick. Bottle, label with the date, and keep it in the fridge. It will keep fermenting very slowly, so burp the bottle for the first week.
recipes.keeps: In the fridge, 3 months or more — the colour dulls before the flavour goes. It is not shelf-stable. If it turns fizzy and foamy again or smells off, compost it.
recipes.variations: Add a carrot or half an onion to the jar for body and sweetness; a few slices of fresh ginger or a strip of lime zest at the blending stage. For a Louisiana-style sauce use only red cayenne and blend with brine alone.

recipes.title: Frozen sweet corn, on the cob and whole kernel
recipes.tagline: Blanched the same day it was picked, August corn tastes like August in February. Kernels for chowder, a few cobs for a treat.
recipes.makes: About 1 kg of kernels from a dozen average ears; a dozen cobs fills a 4 L freezer bag
safety: Blanching is not optional for corn: 4 minutes for kernels, 7–11 minutes on the cob by size. Unblanched corn keeps freezing but turns starchy and stale within weeks.
Time from when the water returns to the boil, not from when the corn goes in. Use enough water (4 L per 450 g) so it recovers fast.
Cool as long as you blanched, in ice water, and drain thoroughly — wet corn freezes as a block with ice crystals through it.
Freeze no more than will go solid within 24 hours (roughly 1–1.5 kg per 30 L of freezer space at a time), with packages spread out until frozen.
ingredients: Sweet corn picked that morning if you can — it loses sugar by the hour
A large pot of boiling water: 4 L (1 gallon) per 450 g (1 lb) of corn
A sink or tub of ice water: about 450 g of ice per 450 g of corn
