steps: Shuck the corn and pull off the silk — the best job in the garden for a child, outside, over the compost. Trim any wormy tips.
Bring the big pot to a rolling boil. Lower in a few ears at a time without crowding so the water comes back to the boil quickly.

For corn on the cob, time from when the water returns to the boil: small ears (3.2 cm, 1¼ inches across or less) 7 minutes, medium (3.2–3.8 cm) 9 minutes, large (over 3.8 cm, 1½ inches) 11 minutes. For whole kernel corn, blanch the ears 4 minutes.
Lift the ears straight into the ice water and leave them there as long as they boiled. Cobs must be chilled to the core or the frozen corn tastes of cob; swap in fresh ice as it melts.

Drain well. For cobs: pat dry, wrap each in plastic or pack several in a freezer bag, press out the air, seal and freeze. For kernels: stand each ear in a wide bowl and cut down with a sharp knife about two-thirds the depth of the kernel, leaving the tough base on the cob.
Pack the kernels into freezer bags or boxes leaving 1.25 cm (½ inch) headspace, press out the air, label with the date and freeze flat so they stack.
recipes.keeps: 8–12 months at −18 °C (0 °F) for best quality. Cook kernels from frozen; thaw cobs in the fridge before boiling or they cook unevenly.
recipes.variations: For cream-style corn, blanch 4 minutes, cut just the kernel tips, then scrape the cobs with the back of the knife to get the milk; pack with 1.25 cm headspace. Leftover cobs make a sweet stock for chowder — simmer 30 minutes and freeze that too.

recipes.title: Frozen green beans and peas
recipes.tagline: The two crops that come all at once and go over in days. Three minutes in boiling water for beans, a minute and a half for peas, and they are saved.
recipes.makes: About 1 kg of beans fills three 1 L freezer bags; 1 kg of pea pods gives about 400 g of shelled peas
recipes.total: 1 hour including shelling, cooling and packing
safety: Blanching times are the recipe: beans 3 minutes, peas 1½ minutes, counted from when the water returns to the boil. Under-blanched vegetables keep their enzymes and go tough and dull-coloured in the freezer; over-blanched ones go mushy.
Use plenty of water — 4 L per 450 g — so the boil recovers fast, and chill in ice water for the same number of minutes.
Drain well. Surface water turns into a block of ice and freezer burn.
Do not add salt or butter before freezing; season when you cook them.
ingredients: Young, tender green or wax beans with the seeds just forming, and/or peas picked while the pods are full but still sweet
A large pot of boiling water: 4 L (1 gallon) per 450 g (1 lb) of vegetables
A tub of ice water: about 450 g of ice per 450 g of vegetables
steps: Wash the beans in cold water, snip off the ends and cut or snap into 5–10 cm (2–4 inch) pieces. Shell the peas. Both are perfect jobs for a child at the table with a bowl in their lap.
Bring the big pot to a hard boil. Add no more than 450 g of vegetables at a time so the water comes back to the boil within a minute.
Time from when the water returns to the boil: beans 3 minutes, peas 1½ minutes. Keep beans and peas in separate batches — their times are different.

Lift them out with a strainer basket straight into the ice water and chill for the same time they boiled (3 minutes for beans, 1½ for peas). Scoop them out and drain thoroughly in a colander, shaking off the water.
Spread on a clean tea towel and pat dry. Pack into freezer bags or boxes leaving 1.25 cm (½ inch) headspace, press out the air, seal and label.
Lay the bags flat in a single layer on a freezer shelf until solid, then stack. For loose, scoopable peas, freeze them first on a tray and bag once hard.
recipes.keeps: 8–12 months at −18 °C (0 °F). Cook from frozen in a little boiling water or straight into soup; thawing first makes them soggy.
recipes.variations: Sugar-snap and snow peas in the pod blanch 1½–3 minutes depending on size. Steam blanching takes about half again as long as water blanching.

recipes.title: Whole tomatoes, frozen without blanching
recipes.tagline: The zero-effort way to save tomatoes on a night you have none to spare: wash, core, bag. The skins slip off under the tap in January.
recipes.makes: A 4 L freezer bag holds about 2 kg of medium tomatoes
safety: Tomatoes are one of the few vegetables that need no blanching before freezing; the skins come off after instead.
They will be soft and watery when thawed. Frozen tomatoes are for cooking — sauce, soup, stew — not salads or slicing.
Freeze them bare. Garlic, onion and herbs change in the freezer, some stronger and some weaker; season when you cook.
Use freezer bags or freezer-grade boxes, not bread bags or yogurt tubs, which let moisture out and freezer burn in.

source.label: University of Nebraska–Lincoln Extension: Freezing tomatoes (whole, with peels)

ingredients: Firm, ripe tomatoes of any kind — paste types freeze with less water, but slicers and cherry tomatoes are fine
Nothing else
steps: Sort the tomatoes and set aside any that are split or soft for tonight’s supper. Rub the rest clean under cold running water and dry them with a towel — a child can wash and dry while you core.
Cut out the stem scar and the hard core around it with the tip of a paring knife.
Set the whole tomatoes, not touching, on a baking sheet and freeze until rock hard, usually overnight.
Tip the frozen tomatoes into freezer bags, press out as much air as you can, seal and label with the date. Return to the freezer at once.

To use, run a frozen tomato under warm water for a few seconds and the skin slides off in your hand. Drop into soup, sauce or chili frozen, or thaw in a bowl and pour off the extra liquid for a thicker sauce.
recipes.keeps: About 8 months at −18 °C (0 °F) for best quality. Cook straight from frozen, or thaw in the fridge and use the same day.
recipes.variations: Cherry tomatoes freeze the same way and go into a pan whole to roast from frozen. If you would rather peel first, dip in boiling water about 1 minute until the skins split, slip them, then tray-freeze as above.

recipes.title: Roasted peppers, frozen
recipes.tagline: Char them while the grill is still out, then pull a bag of smoky strips for pizza or chili all winter. Sweet or hot, same method.
recipes.makes: About 1 kg of fresh peppers gives 500–600 g of roasted strips, enough for four 250 ml tubs
safety: Hot peppers: gloves, and glasses if you are grilling a lot of them. Capsaicin oil in the eyes or under fingernails hurts for hours, and the smoke off a grill full of chiles makes people cough.
Cool roasted peppers to fridge temperature within 2 hours and freeze them within 3 days — a warm bowl of roasted peppers is a good place for bacteria to grow.
Roasting is a quality step, not a preservation one. Freezing is what keeps them; roasted peppers at room temperature are not safe.
Peppers are low-acid, so this frozen recipe is the simple route. Canning them needs a pressure canner and NCHFP’s tested peppers recipe, which these roasted strips are not.
Do not store them under oil in the fridge or the cupboard: peppers or garlic in oil is a botulism risk unless frozen.

source.label: Colorado State University Extension (Food Smart Colorado): Processing roasted chile peppers

ingredients: Thick-walled sweet peppers, or hot peppers such as Anaheim, poblano, Hungarian wax or jalapeño — any quantity
Nothing else; season when you cook with them
steps: Wash the peppers and leave them whole. For hot peppers, put on gloves and keep children away from the cutting board — they can help later with the labelling. Prick thick peppers once with a knife so they do not burst.

Blister the skins over high heat: on a hot grill, under the broiler on the top rack, or directly over a gas burner, turning with tongs until the skin is blackened and puffed on all sides. A slow roast over a flame gives a sweeter, smokier result than a fast one.
Drop the hot peppers into a covered bowl or a food-grade bag and let them steam 10–15 minutes; the skins loosen and the flesh finishes cooking.

Peel if you like — the charred skin rubs off with your fingers or a paper towel, rinsing lightly if needed — then pull out the stem and seeds and tear or slice into strips. Or skip peeling: whole roasted peppers frozen in their skins are easier to peel once thawed.
Cool the peppers quickly — spread on a tray in the fridge or over a bowl of ice — and get them cold within 2 hours of roasting. If they wait in the fridge, use or freeze them within 3 days.
Pack in freezer bags with the air pressed out, or in rigid tubs with 1.25 cm (½ inch) headspace. Pack in meal-sized amounts; label sweet and hot clearly and freeze.
recipes.keeps: Best within a year at −18 °C (0 °F). Use from frozen in cooked dishes, or thaw in the fridge; the strips will be soft.
recipes.variations: Unroasted peppers freeze too: halve or slice sweet peppers and freeze raw with no headspace for crunch-free cooking use, or blanch halves 3 minutes and strips 2 minutes for a softer result. Hot peppers freeze whole and raw, stems off.

recipes.title: Roasted squash and pumpkin purée, frozen
recipes.tagline: The safe way to put up smooth pumpkin for pie, soup and muffins — in the freezer, in the amounts your recipes call for.
recipes.makes: A 2 kg butternut or pie pumpkin gives about 1 L of purée, four 250 ml portions
safety: This is the home route for smooth pumpkin. Purée cannot be canned safely at home at any pressure or time — it is too thick and too variable for heat to penetrate predictably — so it goes in the freezer or it goes in cubes in a pressure canner.
Cook until fully soft and cool quickly before packing; a big warm tub of purée takes hours to chill in the middle.
Leave 1.25 cm headspace in rigid containers — purée expands as it freezes and will pop a lid.
Thaw in the fridge, not on the counter, and use within a few days of thawing.
ingredients: Mature winter squash or pie pumpkin with a hard rind — butternut, buttercup, kabocha, hubbard, sugar pumpkin
Nothing else: no sugar, salt or spice until you bake
steps: Heat the oven to 200 °C (400 °F). Wash the squash, halve it with a heavy knife (the adult’s job) and scoop out the seeds and strings with a spoon — the child’s job, with the seeds set aside for roasting.

Lay the halves cut-side down on a lined baking sheet and roast until a knife slides into the thickest part with no resistance, 45–75 minutes depending on size. You can boil, steam or pressure-cook chunks instead; roasting just tastes better and drives off water.
Scoop the flesh from the rind and mash with a potato masher, or purée in a food processor for pie-smooth texture. If it looks watery, drain it in a sieve for half an hour.
Set the pot or bowl of purée in a sink of cold water and stir now and then until it is cool to the touch — do not pack it warm.
Measure into freezer boxes or bags in the amounts your recipes use (a 540 ml tin of pumpkin is about 2 cups), leaving 1.25 cm (½ inch) headspace in boxes. Press bags flat and squeeze out the air.
Label with squash type, amount and date, and freeze flat until solid before stacking.
recipes.keeps: 8–12 months at −18 °C (0 °F). Thawed purée weeps liquid; pour it off or stir it back in depending on the recipe. Use within 3–4 days of thawing.
recipes.variations: Freeze some of it already seasoned as pie filling base (purée, brown sugar, spice) if you know it is only ever going into pie. Freeze 2-tablespoon blobs in an ice-cube tray for stirring into a toddler’s porridge.

recipes.title: Basil pesto cubes, frozen
recipes.tagline: Pick the basil before the first frost night takes it, blitz it, freeze it in cubes. One cube on hot pasta in February is the whole point of the herb bed.
recipes.makes: About 375 ml of pesto, 24 ice-cube-tray cubes, from 2 cups of leaves
safety: Pesto is garlic and herbs in oil, and oil keeps the air out: exactly the conditions in which Clostridium botulinum grows at room temperature or in a slow fridge. Fresh pesto is a fridge food for no more than 3 days; anything beyond that must be frozen.
Never leave the jar on the counter or in a cupboard, and do not top it with oil and call it preserved.
Thaw in the fridge and eat within a day or two; do not refreeze.
Wash and dry the basil thoroughly — soil on the leaves is the usual source of spores, and water in the paste shortens even its fridge life.
ingredients: 500 ml (2 cups) packed fresh basil leaves, stems removed
125 ml (½ cup) olive oil
60 ml (¼ cup) pine nuts, walnuts or sunflower seeds
2 cloves garlic
¼ teaspoon (1 ml) salt
Optional, best added after thawing: 125 ml (½ cup) finely grated Parmesan
steps: Pick the basil in the morning, before it is wilted by sun or blackened by frost. Have a child strip the leaves off the stems into a colander; rinse and spin or pat them completely dry — water makes grey pesto.
Put the basil, nuts, garlic and salt in a food processor and pulse until finely chopped, scraping down the sides.

With the motor running, pour in the oil in a thin stream until you have a loose, spoonable paste. Leave the cheese out if you plan to freeze it — it stirs in better after thawing, and the pesto freezes cleaner without it.
Spoon into an ice-cube tray, smooth the tops and film the surface with a little extra oil to slow browning. Or pack into small freezer jars with 1.25 cm (½ inch) headspace.
Freeze overnight. Pop the cubes out and move them into a labelled freezer bag, squeezing out the air. Any pesto not going into the freezer goes in the fridge now and gets eaten within 3 days.
To use, drop a cube or two into hot drained pasta or a soup pot, or thaw in the fridge and stir in the cheese.
recipes.keeps: Up to a year at −18 °C (0 °F); the colour darkens before the flavour fades. In the fridge, 3 days, no more.
recipes.variations: Swap half the basil for parsley or arugula to stretch a thin harvest; make a garlic-scape version in June with the same method. For plain frozen basil, chop the leaves, pack into cube trays with just enough water or oil to bind, and freeze — the same 3-day fridge rule applies to the oil version.

recipes.title: Tray-frozen berries: raspberries, strawberries, haskap
recipes.tagline: No sugar, no syrup, nothing to measure — a single layer on a tray, then a bag you can pour from. The way to save a picking before it moulds overnight.
recipes.makes: A standard baking sheet holds about 1 kg of berries per freezing round
recipes.total: 3–4 hours to freeze hard, then bag
safety: Tray-freeze and bag promptly: berries left loose in the freezer freezer-burn within days. The quality rule here is the whole method.
Freeze no more than will go hard within 24 hours, in single layers; a deep bowl of berries freezes slowly and bleeds juice.
Thawed berries are soft and weep juice — they are for cooking, baking and blending, not a fruit plate. Do not refreeze a thawed bag.
Wash before freezing, not after; frozen berries thaw too fast under the tap.

source.label: NCHFP: Dry or tray packing for fruits

ingredients: Fully ripe, firm berries — raspberries, strawberries or haskap — picked dry if possible
Nothing else
steps: Sort the berries and pull out leaves, stems and any that are mushy or mouldy; those go to the chickens or the compost. Children are good at this, especially if allowed to eat the rejects.
Rinse gently in a colander under cold water and drain well. Spread on a clean towel and let them dry for a few minutes — wet berries freeze with a frost coat and clump.
Hull strawberries with a paring knife or the tip of a teaspoon; leave raspberries and haskap whole.
Spread in a single layer, not touching, on a parchment-lined baking sheet. Slide onto a flat freezer shelf.

As soon as they are hard — usually 2–4 hours — pour them into labelled freezer bags or boxes, press out the air and seal. Do not leave them on the open tray overnight or they dry out and pick up freezer smells.
Pour out what you need and reseal the bag. Use from frozen in porridge, muffins, pancakes and smoothies; thaw in the fridge for sauce.
recipes.keeps: 8–12 months at −18 °C (0 °F). Haskap and raspberries keep their flavour best; strawberries soften most on thawing.
recipes.variations: For a sweeter pack NCHFP gives a sugar pack: 175 ml (¾ cup) sugar stirred gently into each litre (about 600 g) of berries until it dissolves, then packed with headspace. Sliced strawberries hold their shape better in sugar than whole ones. Haskap behave like blueberries in the freezer and in every muffin recipe.

recipes.title: Dried apple rings
recipes.tagline: Leathery, chewy, lunchbox-sized apple: the drying recipe to start with, because it forgives almost everything except skipping the dip.
recipes.makes: About 500 g of dried rings from 5 kg of fresh apples (they lose about nine-tenths of their weight)
recipes.total: 6–12 hours in a dehydrator, plus 4–10 days of conditioning
safety: The ascorbic-acid or lemon dip is what stops the apples browning and losing flavour and vitamin C; Colorado State also counts it as an antimicrobial step that helps destroy bacteria during drying, so do not skip it.
Dry at 60 °C (140 °F) — hotter case-hardens the outside and traps moisture inside, which is where mould starts weeks later.
Condition for 4–10 days before you put the jar away. Any sign of condensation means back into the dehydrator; any mould during storage means the whole jar is compost.
Store cool, dry and dark in airtight containers. Warm storage halves the shelf life.

source.label: Colorado State University Extension, PreserveSmart: Drying apples

ingredients: Firm, ripe apples — any amount; crisp tart kinds (Cortland, Honeycrisp, Empire, Liberty) dry best

Anti-browning dip, choose one: 1 teaspoon (5 ml, 3 g) ascorbic acid powder stirred into 500 ml (2 cups) cold water; or equal parts bottled lemon juice and cold water; or 1 teaspoon (5 g) citric acid in 1 L (1 quart) cold water
steps: Wash the apples. Peel if you like (the skins go leathery but are fine to eat), core, and slice into rings 3–6 mm (⅛–¼ inch) thick — a mandoline or an apple peeler-corer keeps them even. Cut out any bruises.
Drop the slices into the dip as you go and let them soak 3–5 minutes. A child can be in charge of the dipping bowl, pushing the rings under with a spoon.
Drain the rings in a colander and blot on a towel. Lay them in a single layer on the dehydrator trays without overlapping.
Dry at 60 °C (140 °F). Plan on 6–12 hours, turning the trays around halfway if your dehydrator dries unevenly. In an oven, use the lowest setting with the door cracked and expect up to twice as long.
Test a cooled ring, not a warm one: it should be leathery and pliable, bending without snapping and with no wet spot when torn in half. Err on the dry side.

Cool completely, then condition: pack loosely into a glass jar, seal, and leave 4–10 days on the counter, shaking daily. If moisture beads on the glass, dry them longer. This evens out the moisture between pieces and is what stops mould.
Pack into airtight jars or freezer bags in amounts you will use within a week or two of opening, label, and store cool and dark.
recipes.keeps: 6–12 months in a cool, dark cupboard — closer to a year at 16 °C (60 °F), six months at 27 °C (80 °F). Once opened, use within a few weeks and watch for softening.
recipes.variations: A pinch of cinnamon shaken over the trays before drying. Pears dry the same way at the same temperature. For a crisp apple chip, slice paper-thin and dry until brittle, and condition them like the rings.

recipes.title: Fruit leather, apple or berry
recipes.tagline: Purée poured thin and dried into a roll-up: the snack children ask for by name, made from the fruit that was too soft for anything else.
recipes.makes: 500 ml (2 cups) of purée makes one 33 × 38 cm (13 × 15 inch) sheet, about 8 roll-ups
recipes.total: 6–8 hours in a dehydrator, up to 18 in an oven
safety: Dry at 60 °C (140 °F) until there is no indentation in the centre. A tacky middle means moisture, and moisture means mould within a few weeks.
Use plastic wrap or a purpose-made sheet to line the tray, never waxed paper or foil.
The lemon juice or ascorbic acid for apple leather is to keep the colour; sweetener is optional and does not affect keeping.
At room temperature it lasts about a month; for longer, the freezer. If a roll ever smells fermented or shows spots, discard it.
ingredients: 500 ml (2 cups) fruit purée per sheet: ripe or slightly overripe apples, strawberries, raspberries, haskap, or a mix — stems, peels and seeds removed
For light-coloured fruit (apple, pear): 2 teaspoons (10 ml) lemon juice or ⅛ teaspoon (375 mg) ascorbic acid per 500 ml of purée
Optional sweetener: 60–125 ml (¼–½ cup) honey, sugar or corn syrup per 500 ml purée, to taste
Optional spice: start with ⅛ teaspoon (0.5 ml) cinnamon or similar per 500 ml purée
steps: Wash the fruit in cool water. Peel and core apples and simmer the chunks with a splash of water until soft; berries can be used raw. Pull out stems and any bad spots — a child can hull and sort while you cook.
Purée until completely smooth in a blender or food processor. Stir in the lemon juice or ascorbic acid for pale fruit, and sweetener and spice if using. For seedy raspberries, press through a sieve.
Line the dehydrator tray or a rimmed baking sheet with plastic wrap or the dehydrator’s fruit-leather sheet, smoothing out wrinkles. Do not use waxed paper or foil — the leather welds to them.
Pour on the purée and spread it about 3 mm (⅛ inch) thick, a little thicker at the edges, which dry first. 500 ml covers a 33 × 38 cm sheet.
Dry at 60 °C (140 °F): roughly 6–8 hours in a dehydrator, up to 18 hours in an oven on its lowest setting with the door propped open.

It is done when you press the centre and your finger leaves no dent, and the sheet peels from the plastic in one piece. While still warm, peel it off, roll it up in a fresh piece of plastic wrap, and let it cool.
Cut the roll into lengths with scissors — the best part for small helpers — and store in an airtight jar or bag.
recipes.keeps: Up to 1 month at room temperature, tightly wrapped; up to 1 year in the freezer. Keeps longer in the fridge than on the shelf.
recipes.variations: Half apple purée with half berry or rhubarb purée stretches a small berry picking and sets a cleaner leather. Unsweetened applesauce from a jar works as the base. Sprinkle with chopped nuts or coconut before drying for a chewier bar.

recipes.title: Dried herbs, air-dried and dehydrated
recipes.tagline: Bunches of thyme hanging from a nail, basil laid flat in the dehydrator: the whole herb bed in six jars before the frost takes it.
recipes.makes: A loose grocery bag of fresh herbs dries down to one or two 250 ml jars
recipes.total: 1–4 hours in a dehydrator; 1–2 weeks hanging
safety: Tender, juicy herbs — basil, mint, lemon balm, tarragon — mould in a hanging bundle before they dry. They go in the dehydrator or a well-ventilated paper bag.
Keep the dehydrator under 46 °C (115 °F) unless the air is very humid; hotter cooks off the volatile oils you are trying to keep.
A hanging bundle must be small and loose. A thick bunch stays damp in the middle and grows grey mould that you will not see until you crumble it.
Dried herbs are 3–4 times stronger than fresh, so use about a third of the amount a recipe gives for fresh.
ingredients: Sturdy herbs for hanging: rosemary, sage, thyme, summer savory, parsley (dill and coriander seed heads go in a paper bag)
Tender herbs for the dehydrator or the paper-bag method: basil, mint, lemon balm, tarragon, oregano and marjoram leaves, chives
String and a paper bag, or a dehydrator with mesh liners
steps: Cut herbs in the morning once the dew has dried, ideally just before they flower when the oils are strongest. Rinse in cool water, shake off the drops, and throw out anything bruised, dirty or yellow. Children can strip leaves from stems and spot the bad ones.

Hanging method, for the sturdy herbs: tie 5–8 stems in a small bundle with string, hang them upside down somewhere warm, airy and out of the sun — a kitchen beam or a closet — and leave 1–2 weeks until the leaves crumble.

Paper-bag method, for tender or dusty herbs: punch holes in the sides of a paper bag, put a small bundle inside leaves-down, gather the bag around the stems with an elastic, and hang it where air moves. The bag catches falling leaves and keeps dust and light off.

Dehydrator method, best for basil, mint and anything with a lot of moisture: lay leaves or short sprigs in a single layer on the trays and dry at 35–46 °C (95–115 °F), or up to 52 °C (125 °F) in muggy weather, for 1–4 hours. Check after an hour; basil goes from limp to crisp quickly.
They are dry when leaves crumble between your fingers and stems snap rather than bend. Anything still bendy goes back.
Strip the leaves and store them whole — crumble at the stove, not before, to keep the oils in. Pack into small airtight jars, label, and keep in a cool, dark cupboard away from the stove.
Check the jars the first week. Any mist on the glass means they were not fully dry: tip them back onto a tray and dry further.
recipes.keeps: Best flavour within a year; after that they are safe but dull. Store whole, airtight, cool and dark, and never shake a jar over a steaming pot.
recipes.variations: Dill heads and coriander seed hang in a paper bag until the seed drops. Make your own herbes de Provence or an Italian mix once everything is dry. For herbs you use mostly in cooked dishes (parsley, chives, dill), freezing chopped in cubes keeps more of the fresh flavour than drying.

recipes.title: Dried hot peppers and chili flakes
recipes.tagline: A year of chili flakes from a single plant: slice, dry, and crumble. Gloves on, windows open, children at a distance.
recipes.makes: 1 kg of fresh hot peppers gives about 100–150 g dried — a full 500 ml jar of flakes
recipes.total: 8–12 hours in a dehydrator, plus 4–10 days of conditioning
safety: Gloves, always, and do not touch your face. Capsaicin does not wash off with water alone; use soap and oil, then soap again.
Grind and dry with ventilation. Hot-pepper dust in a closed kitchen will send everyone out coughing, and small children are the most affected.
Dry until tough to brittle and condition before storing; a leathery pepper that still has moisture inside moulds in the jar.

A ristra — whole peppers strung and hung to air-dry — only works with thin-walled red peppers in a dry climate. In a humid Quebec or Ontario September the inside rots before the outside dries, so hang them indoors near a dehumidifier or use the dehydrator.

source.label: Colorado State University Extension, PreserveSmart: Drying hot peppers

ingredients: Ripe hot peppers, any kind — cayenne, jalapeño, Thai, habanero, Hungarian wax — firm and unblemished
Disposable or rubber gloves; a pair of glasses does not hurt
steps: Put on gloves before you touch the peppers and keep them on until the trays are loaded. Wash the peppers and drain well. This is one recipe to do while the children are elsewhere; they can help with the labelling at the end.

Cut off the stems. For thick-walled peppers, slice into 0.5–1 cm (¼–⅜ inch) rings or strips; split thin cayenne and Thai types lengthwise. Remove the seeds and membranes for milder flakes, or leave them for heat.
Lay in a single layer on the dehydrator trays, cut side up, not touching.

Dry at 60 °C (140 °F) for 8–12 hours, until the pieces are tough to brittle and snap rather than bend. An oven on its lowest setting with the door cracked takes up to twice as long; run the range hood and open a window, because the air will carry capsaicin.
Cool completely on the trays. Condition in a loosely filled, sealed jar for 4–10 days, shaking daily; if any moisture shows on the glass, dry them longer.
Store whole in airtight jars in a cool dark cupboard, or grind to flakes or powder in a spice grinder in small batches — outdoors or under the hood, and let the dust settle before opening the lid.
recipes.keeps: 6–12 months in a cool dark cupboard for best colour and heat; the freezer keeps them longer. Whole dried peppers hold their flavour better than flakes, and flakes better than powder.
recipes.variations: For a ristra, New Mexico State Extension’s method is to string whole mature red pods through the stems with a needle and heavy thread, hang them stem-up where air moves freely, and wait for shrunken, dark-red, still-flexible pods. Smoke jalapeños on the grill before drying for homemade chipotle. Sweet peppers dry the same way for soup flakes.

recipes.title: Dried cherry and paste tomatoes
recipes.tagline: Halved cherry tomatoes dried to chewy, sweet-sour coins — the concentrated taste of the whole summer in a jar. Kept dry, not in oil.
recipes.makes: About 70–150 g of dried tomatoes from 2 kg of fresh cherry or paste tomatoes
recipes.total: 6–12 hours in a dehydrator, plus 4–10 days of conditioning
safety: Do not store dried tomatoes under oil at room temperature. Oil seals the air out and a low-acid tomato with a little moisture left in it is exactly what Clostridium botulinum needs; store-bought ones are acidified in a factory. If you make an oil-packed jar at home, it lives in the fridge and is eaten within 4 days, or goes in the freezer.
Dry to brittle and condition for 4–10 days before sealing a jar for the cupboard. Pieces that are still pliable belong in the fridge or freezer.
Peeling is a texture choice, not a safety step; the 30-second blanch is just to loosen skins.
Any musty smell, soft spots or mould in the jar: discard the lot.

source.label: Colorado State University Extension, PreserveSmart: Drying tomatoes

ingredients: Ripe cherry tomatoes or paste tomatoes (Roma, San Marzano, Amish Paste) — meaty, low-juice kinds dry fastest and best
Optional: a light sprinkle of salt, or dried oregano or basil, on the cut sides
steps: Wash and dry the tomatoes. Halve cherry tomatoes; slice paste tomatoes 0.5–1 cm (¼–⅜ inch) thick or into quarters lengthwise. Peeling is optional — if you want skinless pieces, dip whole tomatoes 30 seconds in boiling water, then into ice water, and slip the skins first. Colorado State also suggests an optional 3–5 minute dip in 1 teaspoon citric acid per litre of water as an antimicrobial step. A child can halve cherry tomatoes with a table knife.

Scoop the wettest seed gel out of large slices with a fingertip; it only slows the drying. Lay the pieces cut side up in a single layer on the dehydrator trays, and salt or herb the surfaces lightly if you like.

Dry at 60 °C (140 °F) for 6–12 hours — cherry halves toward the short end, thick slices toward the long. In an oven on its lowest setting with the door cracked, expect up to twice as long. Rotate the trays once.
Test a cooled piece. For a shelf-stable jar, dry until crisp and brittle; for a chewy snack texture, stop at leathery and keep those in the fridge or freezer.
Cool completely, then condition: pack loosely in a sealed jar for 4–10 days, shaking daily. If moisture fogs the glass, return them to the dehydrator.

Pack into airtight jars or freezer bags, label, and store in a cool dark cupboard, the fridge or the freezer. Rehydrate in hot water or broth for 20–30 minutes before using, or grind the crisp ones into tomato powder for soups.
recipes.keeps: Crisp-dried and conditioned: 6–12 months in a cool dark cupboard, longer in the freezer. Leathery ones: a few weeks in the fridge, a year in the freezer. Oil-packed: 4 days in the fridge.
recipes.variations: Whole dried cherry tomatoes blitzed with dried basil and salt make a seasoning powder for popcorn. To use them like oil-packed, cover a few days’ worth with olive oil, garlic and herbs in a small jar and keep it in the fridge for 4 days at most.

recipes.title: Strawberry jam with Original Fruit Pectin
recipes.tagline: Canada’s jam. Eight jars in under an hour, set every time, from the berries picked the same morning or from the freezer in January.
recipes.makes: About 8 × 250 ml jars
recipes.total: 1¼ hours including processing; 24 hours to cool and set
safety: The sugar and fruit amounts are the pectin maker’s recipe: 1,250 ml crushed fruit, 1,750 ml sugar, one 57 g package of Original Fruit Pectin. Cutting the sugar with regular pectin gives a runny jam that can mould; for less sugar, use a no-sugar-needed pectin and its own recipe instead.
Powdered and liquid pectins are not interchangeable — they go in at different points and want different sugar. This recipe is for Bernardin Original (powdered) pectin.
Boil hard for exactly 1 minute after the sugar returns it to a rolling boil. Less and it will not set; much more and it goes stiff and dark.
Process the jars in the boiling-water canner the full 10 minutes. Inverting jars or sealing with paraffin wax are not safe substitutes.
Do not double the batch. Jam that is too deep in the pot cannot reach the gel point before it overcooks.

source.label: Bernardin: Classic ‘Easy’ Strawberry Jam (Original Fruit Pectin)

ingredients: 1,250 ml (5 cups) crushed strawberries — about 2.5 L (2½ quarts) whole berries, roughly 1.5–1.7 kg
1,750 ml (7 cups, about 1.4 kg) granulated sugar
60 ml (4 tablespoons) lemon juice
1 package (57 g) Bernardin Original Fruit Pectin (powdered)
½ teaspoon (2 ml) butter or margarine, optional, to cut the foam

process.altitude: Same time for 250 ml jars. Above 305 m (1,000 ft) add 5 min; above 915 m (3,000 ft) add 10 min; above 1,830 m (6,000 ft) add 15 min; above 2,440 m (8,000 ft) add 20 min.

steps: Put 8 clean 250 ml jars on the rack of a boiling-water canner, cover with water and heat to a simmer (82 °C, 180 °F). Wash the lids in hot soapy water and set them aside dry; Bernardin lids are not pre-heated.
Wash and hull the strawberries. Crush them one layer at a time with a potato masher — a child’s job, in a wide bowl — and measure exactly 1,250 ml (5 cups). Measure the sugar into a separate bowl.
Put the crushed berries and lemon juice in a large, deep stainless-steel pot with the butter, and whisk in the pectin until it dissolves.

Over high heat bring to a full rolling boil, one that keeps boiling when you stir. Add all the sugar at once and, stirring constantly, bring it back to a full rolling boil that cannot be stirred down. Boil hard exactly 1 minute, stirring the whole time. Take off the heat and skim the foam.

Ladle the hot jam into one hot jar at a time to 0.5 cm (¼ inch) from the rim. Slide a plastic knife or bubble tool down the inside to free air, adjust the headspace, wipe the rim, centre the lid and screw the band down just until fingertip-tight. Return the jar to the canner and fill the rest.
Make sure the jars are covered by at least 2.5 cm (1 inch) of water, put the lid on and bring to a full rolling boil. Start timing then: 10 minutes at 0–305 m (0–1,000 ft).
Turn off the heat, remove the lid, wait 5 minutes, then lift the jars out without tilting onto a towel. Leave them 24 hours without touching the bands.
Check the seals: a sealed lid curves down and does not flex. Remove the bands, wipe the jars, label and store. Any jar that did not seal goes in the fridge to eat first.
recipes.keeps: Best within a year in a cool dark cupboard; the colour browns after that but the jam is sound while sealed. Refrigerate after opening and use within 3 weeks.
recipes.variations: Frozen strawberries work: thaw, then crush and measure as fresh. For a chunkier jam, crush only half the berries and quarter the rest. Keep everything else exactly the same.

recipes.title: Raspberry jam with liquid pectin
recipes.tagline: The brightest jar on the shelf, from the canes that fruit again in September. Liquid pectin keeps the cooking short and the flavour fresh.
recipes.makes: About 6 × 250 ml jars
recipes.total: 1 hour including processing; 24 hours to cool and set
safety: This is a liquid-pectin recipe: the sugar goes in with the fruit at the start and the pectin at the end. Do not swap in powdered pectin without switching to its recipe, and do not change the 1,000 ml fruit to 1,625 ml sugar ratio.
A full rolling boil, then exactly 1 minute after the pectin goes in. Timing by the clock, not by eye.
Process in a boiling-water canner 10 minutes with the jars fully covered. Open-kettle sealing (hot jam, lid on, no bath) is not safe and often fails to seal.
Skim the foam before filling; foam trapped under the lid can spoil the seal.
ingredients: 1,000 ml (4 cups) prepared raspberries — about 1.5 L of whole berries, crushed; press some or all through a sieve first if you want fewer seeds
1,625 ml (6½ cups, about 1.3 kg) granulated sugar
1 pouch (85 ml) Bernardin Liquid Pectin
½ teaspoon (2 ml) butter or margarine, optional, to reduce foaming

process.altitude: Same time for 250 ml jars. Above 305 m (1,000 ft) add 5 min; above 915 m (3,000 ft) add 10 min; above 1,830 m (6,000 ft) add 15 min; above 2,440 m (8,000 ft) add 20 min.

steps: Put 6 clean 250 ml jars on the rack of a boiling-water canner, cover with water and heat to a simmer (82 °C, 180 °F). Wash the lids and set them aside dry.
Pick over the raspberries and crush them in a bowl with a potato masher — small hands do this well — measuring 1,000 ml (4 cups) when done. Sieve out some seeds first if you prefer.
In a large, deep stainless-steel pot, stir together the crushed fruit, all of the sugar and the butter.

Over high heat, stirring, bring to a full rolling boil that cannot be stirred down. Squeeze in the whole pouch of liquid pectin, return to a full boil and boil hard exactly 1 minute, stirring constantly. Remove from the heat and skim the foam.

Ladle into one hot jar at a time to 0.5 cm (¼ inch) from the rim. Free the air bubbles with a plastic tool, adjust the headspace, wipe the rim, centre the lid and screw the band on fingertip-tight. Return to the canner and repeat.
With the jars covered by at least 2.5 cm (1 inch) of water, put the lid on, bring to a full rolling boil and process 10 minutes at 0–305 m (0–1,000 ft).
Turn off the heat, remove the lid, wait 5 minutes and lift the jars straight up onto a towel. Leave 24 hours, then check that each lid is dished and firm, remove the bands, label and store.
recipes.keeps: Best within a year in a cool dark cupboard. Refrigerate after opening and use within 3 weeks.
recipes.variations: Half raspberries, half blackberries or black raspberries, measured together to the same 1,000 ml. Everbearing fall raspberries make a slightly softer, deeper-flavoured jam than July ones.

recipes.title: Strawberry rhubarb jam with Original Fruit Pectin
recipes.tagline: June in a jar: the first strawberries and the last tender rhubarb, set with powdered pectin so the tartness stays sharp.
recipes.makes: About 6 × 250 ml jars
recipes.total: 1¼ hours including processing; 24 hours to cool and set
safety: Rhubarb leaves are poisonous (oxalic acid). Trim stalks well below the leaf and keep the leaves away from children and the compost bowl that pets get into.

Fruit, sugar and pectin stay at the tested amounts: 875 ml strawberries, 250 ml rhubarb, 1,300 ml sugar, one 57 g package of Original Fruit Pectin. More rhubarb than this changes the set and is not the tested recipe.
Bottled lemon or lime juice — the acidity of fresh citrus varies and the set depends on it.
Powdered pectin goes in before the boil; the sugar after. Boil hard exactly 1 minute. Process 10 minutes in a boiling-water canner.

source.label: Bernardin: Strawberry Rhubarb Spring Festival Jam (Original Fruit Pectin)

ingredients: 875 ml (3½ cups) crushed strawberries — about 2 L (2 quarts) whole berries
250 ml (1 cup) finely chopped rhubarb, about 2 medium stalks
5–10 ml (1–2 teaspoons) finely grated lemon rind, about 1 lemon
50 ml (¼ cup) bottled lemon or lime juice
1 package (57 g) Bernardin Original Fruit Pectin (powdered)
1,300 ml (5¼ cups, about 1.05 kg) granulated sugar
½ teaspoon (2 ml) butter or margarine, optional, to reduce foaming

process.altitude: Same time for 250 ml jars. Above 305 m (1,000 ft) add 5 min; above 915 m (3,000 ft) add 10 min; above 1,830 m (6,000 ft) add 15 min; above 2,440 m (8,000 ft) add 20 min.

steps: Put 6 clean 250 ml jars on the rack of a boiling-water canner, cover with water and heat to a simmer (82 °C, 180 °F). Wash the lids and set them aside dry.

Wash and hull the strawberries and crush them one layer at a time; measure 875 ml (3½ cups). Wash the rhubarb, trim off every bit of leaf, and chop finely; measure 250 ml (1 cup). A child can crush berries while you chop. Measure the sugar into a bowl.
In a large, deep stainless-steel pot, stir together the strawberries, rhubarb, lemon rind, lemon juice, butter and the pectin.

Over high heat bring to a full rolling boil. Add all the sugar at once and, stirring constantly, return to a full rolling boil that cannot be stirred down. Boil hard exactly 1 minute, stirring. Remove from the heat and skim the foam.

Ladle into one hot jar at a time to 0.5 cm (¼ inch) from the rim. Free the bubbles, adjust the headspace, wipe the rim, centre the lid and tighten the band fingertip-tight. Return to the canner and fill the rest.
Cover the jars with at least 2.5 cm (1 inch) of water, lid on, bring to a full rolling boil and process 10 minutes at 0–305 m (0–1,000 ft).
Turn off the heat, take off the lid, wait 5 minutes, lift the jars straight up onto a towel and leave 24 hours. Check the seals, remove the bands, label and store.
recipes.keeps: Best within a year in a cool dark cupboard. Refrigerate after opening and use within 3 weeks.
recipes.variations: Frozen rhubarb and strawberries from June work in October: thaw, chop and crush, and measure as fresh. A vanilla bean split into the pot and fished out before jarring is a popular addition that does not change the recipe.

recipes.title: Haskap freezer jam (no cooking, no canning)
recipes.tagline: Nobody has published a tested canning recipe for haskap, so this one follows Bernardin’s tested freezer-jam method for blueberries instead: raw fruit, freezer pectin, ten minutes, and it tastes exactly like the berry.
recipes.makes: About 5 × 250 ml jars
safety: This is a freezer jam. There is no tested water-bath recipe for haskap from Bernardin, NCHFP or a Canadian university or provincial lab, and a recipe for a different fruit cannot be assumed to carry over to a jar on the shelf. Freezer jam does not rely on acidity or a seal, so the substitution is safe here.
It is not shelf-stable: in the fridge up to 3 weeks, in the freezer up to a year. Do not process it in a canner — this pectin and this sugar level are not designed for it.
Use Bernardin Freezer Jam Pectin specifically. Regular, liquid and no-sugar-needed pectins each want their own recipe and sugar.
Leave 1 cm headspace; the jam expands as it freezes and will crack a glass jar filled to the brim.

source.label: Bernardin: Blueberry Freezer Jam — Freezer Jam Pectin (followed with haskap in place of blueberries; no tested canned haskap recipe exists)

ingredients: 1,000 ml (4 cups) crushed haskap — about 2 L of whole berries, roughly 1.2 kg
10 ml (2 teaspoons) lightly packed, finely grated orange zest, optional
375 ml (1½ cups, about 300 g) granulated sugar
1 pouch (45 g) Bernardin Freezer Jam Pectin
steps: Wash and rinse 5 Bernardin freezer jars with lids, or 250 ml mason jars with plastic storage lids. Rinse the haskap and pick out stems.
Crush the berries thoroughly by hand with a potato masher, or pulse in a food processor without puréeing — a child can mash. Measure 1,000 ml (4 cups) into a shallow pan.

Optional but worth it: heat the crushed fruit on the stove or in the microwave, stirring, just until it comes to a boil. It deepens the colour and flavour and softens the skins. Stir in the orange zest and set aside.
In a large bowl stir the sugar and the freezer-jam pectin together until evenly mixed.
Pour the fruit into the pectin-sugar mixture and stir for a full 3 minutes by the clock.
Ladle into the jars leaving 1 cm (½ inch) headspace, wipe the rims and put the lids on tightly. Leave on the counter about 30 minutes to thicken.
Label with the date and put the jars in the freezer, keeping out one for the fridge to eat now.
recipes.keeps: Up to 3 weeks in the fridge; up to 1 year in the freezer. Thaw in the fridge overnight and stir before serving.
recipes.variations: Haskap plus rhubarb, measured together to 1,000 ml, is the classic Prairie pairing.
